title: Breaking down Falcons 2026 acquisitions through the bye
summary: The Atlanta Falcons made a lot of roster moves this offseason. I bet you forgot about several of the players on the list I’m about to roll out. With the bye over and Week 12 looming, I thought I’d look back at everyone the Falcons acquired this offseason—I hope, let me know if I missed […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - SEPTEMBER 20: Atlanta Falcons general manager Ian Cunningham reacts prior to the start of the NFL game between the Carolina Panthers and the Atlanta Falcons on September 20th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Atlanta Falcons made a lot of roster moves this offseason. I bet you forgot about several of the players on the list I’m about to roll out. With the bye over and Week 12 looming, I thought I’d look back at everyone the Falcons acquired this offseason—I hope, let me know if I missed a name or two—and talk a little bit about where they are now, how they’ve fared, and in some cases whether they fit into the team’s plans next year. Join me for a leisurely stroll through Ian Cunningham’s first offseason in Atlanta, won’t you? We won’t focus on in-season moves here, and will instead zero in on what the Falcons planned for before the season began. Trade acquisitions DL Gervon Dexter: He’s been as good as you can ask for, and the price was cheap. Dexter is 10th in the NFL in pressures from interior defensive linemen, per Pro Football Focus, is playing some of the best run defense of his career, and has formed a lethal duo with Brandon Dorlus. Considering he’s still quite young, Dexter should be a wrecking ball for years to come, and is probably the crown jewel of Ian Cunningham’s roster machinations in 2026. DL Maason Smith: He’s been overshadowed by Dorlus and Dexter—and for good reason, given that his run defense has been patchily effective and he’s missed tackles—but Smith is offering some real juice as a pass rusher and has been at worst a really solid addition to the rotation up front. S/CB Sydney Brown: A versatile defensive back who has played well overall, Brown was acquired in a pick swap with the Eagles where Philadelphia got a pair of solid pick upgrades on day three. Filling in at safety, nickel cornerback, and even outside in a pinch, Brown’s well-rounded game allows him to fill many roles for Atlanta, and I have to think he’ll be re-signed in 2027. This might be Cunningham’s strongest work. Dexter has been a home run addition and Smith a good one, especially as an upgrade over Ruke Orhorhoro, who this coaching staff had seemingly soured on, and Brown has been a glue guy for a secondary that has otherwise been scuffling this year. Two capable, young defensive linemen for two players you weren’t planning to utilize (Ruke and Clark Phillips), two pick swaps, and a fifth round pick is good value. Free agents/waivers QB Tua Tagovailoa: He basically hasn’t played, finishing the Ravens game by throwing a game-ending interception, with injuries flaring up when he had a chance to start instead of Michael Penix Jr. He has cost the Falcons basically nothing but won’t be back next year. QB Trevor Siemian: A reliable enough if noodle-armed thrower who was supposed to be Atlanta’s QB3, Siemian got hurt at the absolute worst time and was waived to make room for Cooper Rush. QB Cooper Rush: Now with the Buccaneers, Atlanta’s emergency third quarterback had to make two starts to begin the campaign and was abysmal. You don’t expect your third QB to have to play extended action and you certainly expect a veteran like Rush to be better than that , but woof. RB Brian Robinson Jr.: He was an excellent complement to Bijan Robinson who also largely proved to be an asset as a kick returner, giving the Falcons their money’s worth. Unfortunately he’s injured and I’m not sure when we’ll see him next. RB Tyler Goodson: After a great summer in Atlanta, Goodson looked like a great signing as the team’s RB3. The Falcons thought they could get away with having him on the practice squad and only carrying two running backs, though, and unfortunately he was poached by the Dallas Cowboys. WR Jahan Dotson: Reviving a moribund career in Atlanta, Dotson is well on his way to a new career high for receiving yards and has used his speed to great effect on a few deep routes. The volume isn’t there, but he’s leading the NFL in yards per catch and should be a favored deep target in 2027 even if he’s WR3. WR Olamide Zaccheaus: A fan favorite during his last stint in Atlanta, OZ has been a disappointing signing who has not been productive as a receiver or returner. This will likely be his last ride in Atlanta. TE Austin Hooper: A situationally useful pass catching tight end and another fun blast from the past, Hooper has made the most of limited opportunities. I imagine the Falcons will be looking for a tight end upgrade, so even though Hooper has been solid, I can’t say I expect him to be back in 2027. TE Nick Muse: A situationally useful blocking tight end and quality special teamer, Muse offers solid value at the bottom of the roster. RT Jawaan Taylor: Still capable in pass protection, Taylor has fallen into familiar bad habits in terms of pre-snap penalties and has not been an asset in run blocking, making his stay in Atlanta a short one in all likelihood. OT Cameron Williams: We haven’t seen him yet, but he’s a reasonably young project for Bill Callahan. C Corey Levin: The jury’s still out on Levin since we’ve only seen one game with him starting, but he’s been a solid sixth lineman when called upon and did better than I would have expected against the Chiefs last week in his first start in years. He might return as the backup next year given that he’s a Bill Callahan favorite. DL Da’Shawn Hand: He was supposed to be a run-stopping anchor in the middle of Atlanta’s defensive line and is sorely missed now; Hand left after a handful of snaps in Week 1 and is out for the season with an injury. DL Chris Williams: He was expected to deliver some pass rushing juice on the interior, but the Falcons went out and got Dexter and Smith and let him go. Williams is currently on the Las Vegas practice squad. EDGE Jared Ivey: He spent a little time with Atlanta on the active roster after he was claimed on waivers, but was phased out of the rotation and ultimately landed on the Falcons practice squad. EDGE Samson Ebukam: The bet on Ebukam was that he would bounce back further away from a rough injury that cost him the entire 2024 season, and that was a good bet. His 2.5 sacks are not eye-popping stuff, but he’s generated pressure; the problem is that he’s currently injured. EDGE Za’Darius Smith : He’s been one of the team’s most effective pass rushers on a per-snap basis, but is playing sparingly for this defense. Still a solid signing for a team that needed help off the edge. EDGE Cameron Thomas : Recently extended, Thomas has been a workhorse for this group and a consistently effective player as a run defender and pass rusher. He has Jeff Ulbrich’s trust and should be one of the team’s most productive defenders down the stretch, too. EDGE Azeez Ojulari: He did not make the final Falcons roster after a quiet summer and is currently hanging out on the Las Vegas practice squad. EDGE Yasir Abdullah: We’ve seen stretches of really good play from Abdullah, who has been typically useful on special teams and has been surprisingly effective on defense. We just haven’t seen a ton of him between rotation decisions and injury. LB Christian Harris: Signed as a seasoned player who had the size and athleticism Jeff Ulbrich looks for at linebacker, Harris lost a starting job to Kendal Daniels and ended up buried on the depth chart. He was just cut by the Falcons. LB Josh Woods: One of the team’s most reliable special teamers and a decent fill-in linebacker in an emergency, Woods joined up in late July and is still here doing his thing. LB Channing Tindall : Expected to be a special teams stalwart, Tindall instead gave way to old friend Josh Woods. K Nick Folk: The biggest bust on this list by far. Folk was supposed to give the Falcons a reliable option after three straight years of leading the league in field goal percentage, but instead he fell apart and cost Atlanta games with…

title: Three former Falcons advance in Pro Football Hall of Fame voting
summary: The voting process for the Pro Football Hall of Fame’s Class of 2027 is underway, as the Hall continues to narrow down its list of candidates ahead of February’s NFL Honors. On Tuesday, the Hall announced that 52 players have advanced to the next round of voting, with three former Atlanta Falcons among them, all […]
full_text: Atlanta Facons linebacker Tommy Nobis during a 1973 game at Atlanta Fulton County Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Bob Verlin/Getty Images) *** Local Caption *** The voting process for the Pro Football Hall of Fame’s Class of 2027 is underway, as the Hall continues to narrow down its list of candidates ahead of February’s NFL Honors. On Tuesday, the Hall announced that 52 players have advanced to the next round of voting, with three former Atlanta Falcons among them, all of whom are deserving of a spot in Canton: Tommy Nobis, John Abraham and Billy “White Shoes” Johnson. Tommy Nobis It’s long overdue for “Mr. Falcon” to receive his gold jacket. The first-ever draft selection in franchise history, Nobis spent his entire 11-year NFL career with the Falcons from 1966-1976. Nobis was named NFL Rookie of the Year in 1966, earned five trips to the Pro Bowl and was named to the NFL’s 1960s All-Decade Team, despite entering the league midway through the decade. He led the Falcons in tackles in nine of his 11 seasons and was an inaugural member of the Falcons Ring of Honor in 2004. His No. 60 jersey is also retired by the franchise. John Abraham One of the best pass rushers in franchise history, Abraham spent seven seasons with the Falcons from 2006-2012, recording 68.5 sacks during his time in Atlanta, which remains an official franchise record. Abraham finished his 15-year NFL career with 133.5 sacks, five Pro Bowl selections and two first-team All-Pro selections. “The Predator” recently received some well-deserved recognition from the franchise, as he was inducted into the Falcons Ring of Honor in October. Billy “White Shoes” Johnson One of the most electrifying return specialists in NFL history, Johnson spent six seasons with the Falcons from 1982-1987. In 1983, Johnson earned his third career Pro Bowl selection and was named NFL Comeback Player of the Year. He also led the Falcons in receptions in both 1983 and 1985. Perhaps most baffling is the fact that Johnson remains the only player named to the NFL’s 75th Anniversary All-Time Team who has yet to be inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. He was also named to the NFL’s 100th Anniversary All-Time Team, as well as the 1970s and 1980s All-Decade Teams. The list of 52 nominees will be narrowed down to 25 following the next round of voting, with the results expected to be announced in approximately two weeks. Hopefully, all three former Falcons will find themselves one step closer to football immortality in Canton, Ohio.

title: AFC North Preview, Week 12: Browns off their bye week, Steelers and Ravens reeling
summary: Updated Standings: Pittsburgh Steelers Matchup: vs. Denver Broncos, 3:00pm EST (Friday) The Steelers were upset by the Philadelphia Eagles last week, dropping their second straight game and falling to 6-4 on the season. Looking to right the ship, the Steelers made a surprising decision to bench quarterback Aaron Rodgers for this week’s game and will […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - NOVEMBER 15: Quarterback Deshaun Watson #4 of the Cleveland Browns celebrates after running for a touchdown during the second quarter against the Houston Texans at Huntington Bank Field on November 15, 2026, in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Updated Standings: Cincinnati Bengals 7-3 Pittsburgh Steelers 6-4 Cleveland Browns 6-4 Baltimore Ravens 4-7 Pittsburgh Steelers Matchup: vs. Denver Broncos, 3:00pm EST (Friday) The Steelers were upset by the Philadelphia Eagles last week, dropping their second straight game and falling to 6-4 on the season. Looking to right the ship, the Steelers made a surprising decision to bench quarterback Aaron Rodgers for this week’s game and will start Mason Rudolph instead. Rodgers’ benching may be a disciplinary action just as much as it as performance-based, but nonetheless it represents a big shift for the Steelers’ offense. Rudolph may have a difficult time getting Pittsburgh’s offense going against an elite Denver Broncos’ defense. While Rodgers hasn’t played great recently, the Steelers’ offensive issues stem beyond just quarterback play — as their supporting cast has been underwhelming. For Rudolph to have a chance to pull off an upset in Week 12, the Steelers will need to block well up front and get a big performance from Jaylen Warren on the ground. Defensively, the key for the Steelers may be slowing down rookie running back Jonah Coleman, who has quickly emerged as the engine of Denver’s offensive attack. Bo Nix has played better at quarterback lately, but the Steelers may be able to force a turnover or two, which frankly may be necessary for them to win. Cincinnati Bengals Matchup: vs. New Orleans Saints, 1:00pm EST The Bengals had their five-game win streak snapped this past Monday night by the Washington Commanders. Despite being favored by more than five points, the Bengals couldn’t get going offensively and allowed a game-winning drive at the end of the fourth quarter. They will look to quickly get back on track with another favorable matchup on hand this week against the New Orleans Saints at home. The Saints are 2-1 against the AFC North this season having been beaten both the Ravens and Browns, which account but for almost all their total victories on the season (three). All five of New Orleans’ recent games have been decided by one possession, so they have a knack for staying within striking distance. The Bengals are favored by 10 points and have the potential to explode offensively at any time. The Saints allow the 10th-most points per game defensively. Cincinnati’s defense, meanwhile, has allowed 22 points or less in three consecutive games, albeit against some softer offenses. The Saints have an inconsistent offensive attack but are not without playmakers, having recently added Travis Etienne and Jordan Tyson into the mix. The Bengals will need to prevent Tyler Shough from finding a rhythm and getting comfortable. Baltimore Ravens Matchup: @ Houston Texans, 1:00pm EST It was another incomplete performance from the Ravens last week, who suffered a sixth straight loss in a 35-33 defeat against the Carolina Panthers. The Ravens could not overcome several miscues including four turnovers and multiple dropped passes. They’ll look to finally right the ship in their final game before a bye week this Sunday, taking on the Houston Texans in a road matchup. Like the Ravens, the Texans are similarly trying to claw their way back to .500 and keep their playoff hopes alive. Houston’s defensive front will challenge the Ravens’ offensive line, particularly in pass protection, where Will Anderson Jr. looms large on the edge. The Ravens will need to find a way to neutralize the Texans’ pass rush to keep Jacoby Brissett upright. On defense, the Ravens continue to struggle allowing pass production over the middle of the field. Their lapses seem to stem mostly from miscommunications in zone coverage and poor execution. Finding a way to tighten things up against the Texans will be a challenge, as C.J. Stroud and company have been a high-octane passing attack this season. Nico Collins is a difficult cover at wide receiver. Cleveland Browns Matchup: vs. Las Vegas Raiders, 8:15pm EST Fresh off their bye week, the Browns will look to keep pushing towards a playoff berth in a primetime home matchup against the Las Vegas Raiders. Cleveland’s defense is in a good spot here hosting a rookie quarterback, Fernando Mendoza, in just his third career start. However, they cannot afford to let their guard down. The Browns’ defense is allowing the sixth-fewest passing yards per game but have been more susceptible against the run, giving up over 126 yards on the ground on average each contest. Fortunately for them, the Raiders have been one of the worst rushing offenses in the league this season, although they did total 143 yards on 6.0 yards per carry last week. Expect the Browns to force Mendoza to beat the blitz and make throws against man coverage. Las Vegas’ defense is plenty vulnerable as well, setting up Deshaun Watson and company to have a good performance. The Browns have continued to struggle to sustain a good run game, as they’ve had a leading rusher exceed 50 yards just three times all season. This is a prime spot for their rushing attack to get going a bit.

Wester, 24, let his first punt return go into the end zone for a touchback on Sunday, but could not handle the second and third balls from Sam […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - NOVEMBER 22: Baltimore Ravens wide receiver LaJohntay Wester (10) misses the catch of a punt during an NFL football game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Carolina Panthers on November 22, 2026 at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. (Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens are waiving second-year wide receiver/returner LaJohntay Wester after two muffed punts in Sunday’s loss to the Carolina Panthers, per Jeff Zrebiec of The Athletic . Wester, 24, let his first punt return go into the end zone for a touchback on Sunday, but could not handle the second and third balls from Sam Martin, both in the second quarter. On the first, he signaled for a fair catch but never settled under the ball, instead attempting a diving grab and letting the ball fall through his arms. The Panthers took over at the Ravens’ 23-yard line and scored a go-ahead touchdown two plays later. The second was significantly worse. Wester had ample time and space to make a clean catch, but the ball ricocheted off his helmet and rolled toward Baltimore’s end zone. Ravens cornerback Keyon Martin managed to corral it at the 1, forcing the offense to battle out of their own end zone with a minute left in the half instead of pushing for another score. Wester did not play another snap for the rest of the game and could be seen on the sidelines being consoled by team chaplain Rev. Johnny Shelton. Carolina only punted one more time with Ravens safety Malaki Starks back to return. He let the ball roll to the 1, where it was downed by a Panther whose heel was on the goal line, resulting in a touchback. This is a breaking story that will be updated with more information.

summary: What do I think the biggest — and specific — defensive key for the Buffalo Bills against the Chiefs on Thanksgiving night? I’ll provide some metrics, and you’ll be able to reach the answer. The Chiefs are: and Patrick Mahomes has the: You guessed it — tackling. The Chiefs, more than any other offense, put […]
full_text: What do I think the biggest — and specific — defensive key for the Buffalo Bills against the Chiefs on Thanksgiving night? I’ll provide some metrics, and you’ll be able to reach the answer. The Chiefs are: First in screen-pass rate in the NFL entering this game at 16.4%, Third in RPO rate at 8.4% and Patrick Mahomes has the: Third-lowest average depth of target (aDOT) at 6.6 yards among 38 qualifiers Fourth-quickest average time to attempt at 2.51 seconds among those same qualifiers Fourth-lowest percentage of throws made 20-plus yards downfield at 9.2% among 33 qualifiers Second-highest adjusted completion percentage at 81.1% You guessed it — tackling. The Chiefs, more than any other offense, put their opponent’s tackling capabilities to the test. How well have the Bills tackled this season, you ask? Below is a graphic that demonstrates the total amount of missed tackles credited to Bills defenders in each game by Pro Football Focus to date this season: After the bye week, which coincides with when CJ Gardner-Johnson was no longer on the team, the Bills have averaged six missed tackles per contest. In the six contests before the bye, Buffalo was averaging 8.5 missed tackles per game. Remember, before the spitting incident in Las Vegas, Gardner-Johnson was the owner of the highest missed tackle rate among qualifying safeties in the NFL. And don’t forget, on August 11, Bills defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard said the following during a press conference on this very topic: “Who can finish, get guys on the ground? That was an Achilles’ heel here last year. So that’s the No. 1 thing we have to correct.” Per PFF, in the regular season, the Bills averaged 8.88 missed tackles per game during the 2025 campaign. In Buffalo’s two playoff outings last season, that figure jumped to 9.5 per. Right now, even with the noticeably bad start, Buffalo’s missed tackles per game average is down to 7.5. And another strong showing in the tackling department for the Bills will go a long way in securing a win over the Chiefs on Thanksgiving night.

title: Buffalo Bills Week 11 game balls: Greg Rousseau and James Cook reach career milestones
summary: The Buffalo Bills took care of business against the Miami Dolphins in Week 11, securing a 26-9 divisional victory at Highmark Stadium before turning their attention to a Thanksgiving night matchup with the Kansas City Chiefs. Buffalo out gained Miami 405-185, controlled the football for 36:45 and held the Dolphins to just two third down […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills took care of business against the Miami Dolphins in Week 11, securing a 26-9 divisional victory at Highmark Stadium before turning their attention to a Thanksgiving night matchup with the Kansas City Chiefs. Buffalo out gained Miami 405-185, controlled the football for 36:45 and held the Dolphins to just two third down conversions on 14 attempts. Perhaps most impressive was the defense’s ability to keep Miami out of the end zone for all four quarters. There was plenty to celebrate in Buffalo’s locker room following Sunday’s victory, including a new career high for one defensive standout and another historic accomplishment for the Bills’ running back. Let’s take a look at who received game balls from head coach Joe Brady before handing out a few of our own. EDGE Greg Rousseau “Look, I could give this to everyone on defense the way y’all are playing right now,” Brady said before awarding his first game ball to Greg Rousseau. And rightfully so. Buffalo’s defense held Miami to just 185 total yards, 10 first downs and three field goals. But Rousseau finished the afternoon with three solo tackles, two sacks, two tackles for loss and two quarterback hits, accounting for both of Buffalo’s sacks and costing the Dolphins a combined 16 yards. His first sack came on Miami’s opening offensive possession when he brought down quarterback Kyle McCord for an eight yard loss on third and six, forcing the Dolphins to punt. With his two sack performance, Rousseau reached 10 sacks on the season, establishing a new career high with six regular season games still to play. Perhaps equally impressive is that Rousseau accomplished all of this while playing just 34 defensive snaps. RB James Cook Brady’s second game ball went to James Cook, who continues to rewrite the NFL record books. Cook finished Sunday’s contest with 22 carries for 89 yards and a touchdown. According to Brady, Cook became the first player in NFL history to record at least 75 rushing yards and a touchdown in nine consecutive games. Brady also recognized Cook for reaching 1,000 rushing yards for the fourth consecutive season. And there’s still plenty of football left to be played. What continues to impress me about Cook is his consistency. Even on an afternoon when Buffalo averaged just 3.5 yards per rushing attempt as a team, Cook found a way to produce and extend his historic streak. Sara’s Game Ball: WR Khalil Shakir and WR DJ Moore I’m going to cheat a little bit this week and award my game ball to two players because, quite frankly, I couldn’t justify recognizing one without the other. Khalil Shakir and DJ Moore combined for 13 receptions on 19 targets for 192 receiving yards and a touchdown, accounting for nearly 63% of quarterback Josh Allen’s 304 passing yards. Shakir hauled in five of nine targets for a team leading 101 receiving yards, averaging an impressive 20.2 yards per reception. Moore, meanwhile, led Buffalo in both receptions (eight) and targets (10), finishing with 91 receiving yards and a touchdown. What stood out most to me about Moore’s performance was his production on third down. Converting on three third downs. While Shakir provided the explosive plays, Moore consistently helped keep the chains moving. Their complementary performances were instrumental in Buffalo’s ability to sustain drives and dominate the time of possession. Both deserve recognition this week. Honorable mentions K Tyler Bass When your kicker accounts for more than half of your team’s points, he certainly deserves some recognition. Bass connected on four of five field goal attempts and both extra point attempts, accounting for 14 of Buffalo’s 26 points. While Buffalo’s inability to consistently finish drives in the end zone remains an area of concern, Bass made sure those possessions didn’t go to waste. P Tommy Doman Imagine making the honorable mentions list as a punter without recording a single punt. Facing fourth and eight from Buffalo’s own 34 yard line in the first quarter, the Bills dialed up a fake punt. Doman connected with tight end Keleki Latu for a 30 yard completion. You can say it… the entire call was borderline disrespectful and I loved every minute of it. RB Ty Johnson While Cook continues to make headlines with his historic rushing performances, Ty Johnson deserves recognition for his contributions to Buffalo’s passing attack. Johnson hauled in seven of eight targets for 55 receiving yards. He finished second on the team in receptions despite playing just 28 offensive snaps. Johnson was particularly effective in helping Buffalo sustain drives. His versatility continues to be a valuable asset to Buffalo’s offense, and Sunday’s performance was another reminder of just how important his role can be. On the the next There’s little time to celebrate, however, with Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs coming to town on Thanksgiving night. Who gets your game balls this week, Bills Mafia?

title: Buffalo Bills Week 11 snap counts: Buffalo dominates time of possession, rotates heavily on defense
summary: The Buffalo Bills defeated the Miami Dolphins 26-9 at Highmark Stadium in Week 11, putting together a dominant defensive performance just four days before they’re scheduled to host the Kansas City Chiefs on Thanksgiving night. Buffalo’s offense accumulated 405 total yards compared to Miami’s 185, while the Bills controlled the time of possession by a […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills defeated the Miami Dolphins 26-9 at Highmark Stadium in Week 11, putting together a dominant defensive performance just four days before they’re scheduled to host the Kansas City Chiefs on Thanksgiving night. Buffalo’s offense accumulated 405 total yards compared to Miami’s 185, while the Bills controlled the time of possession by a margin of 13 minutes and 30 seconds. Let’s take a look at Buffalo’s Week 11 snap counts and some of the more notable personnel decisions. Buffalo Bills offensive snap counts (78 snaps) The Bills ran 21 more offensive snaps than the Dolphins, holding possession of the football for 36:45. Buffalo controlled the clock for nearly 20 minutes in the first half alone, accumulating 254 total yards and 16 first downs while limiting Miami to just 38 yards and two first downs. Despite Buffalo’s ability to sustain drives, the offense converted just two of five red zone opportunities into touchdowns. The Bills didn’t punt once, although punter Tommy Doman contributed to the offensive production with a 30 yard completion to tight end Keleki Latu on a successful fake punt in the first quarter. Offensive line Left tackle Dion Dawkins and left guard Alec Anderson were the only two offensive players to play 100% of Buffalo’s offensive snaps. Center Connor McGovern, right guard O’Cyrus Torrence and right tackle Spencer Brown each played 77 snaps (99%), as did quarterback Josh Allen. Austin Corbett and Tylan Grable each logged three offensive snaps (4%), while Lloyd Cushenberry played one. Wide receivers Keon Coleman and Khalil Shakir led Buffalo’s wide receivers with 63 snaps (81%) apiece, followed by DJ Moore with 58 snaps (74%). While Coleman and Shakir played an identical number of snaps, their production was considerably different. Shakir hauled in five of nine targets for 101 receiving yards, while Coleman caught two of four targets for 17 yards. Moore continued to be heavily involved in Buffalo’s passing attack, leading the team in both targets (10) and receptions (eight) while finishing with 91 receiving yards and a touchdown. Tyrell Shavers, fresh off of the PUP list, logged 29 offensive snaps (37%), while Greg Dortch played just four (5%). Dortch’s biggest contributions came on special teams. Running backs James Cook played just 41 offensive snaps (53%) but handled 22 of Buffalo’s 27 rushing attempts, finishing with 89 rushing yards and a touchdown. The distribution of snaps between Cook and Ty Johnson is particularly interesting when looking at how Buffalo utilized the two running backs. Johnson played 28 offensive snaps (36%), hauling in seven of eight targets for 55 receiving yards. Johnson’s ability to contribute in the passing game gives Buffalo another reliable option when attempting to sustain drives. Ray Davis rounded out the running back rotation with nine offensive snaps (12%). Tight ends Dawson Knox led Buffalo’s tight ends with 47 snaps (60%), followed by Latu with 28 (36%) and Jackson Hawes with 16 (21%). Knox finished with two receptions for 31 yards, while Latu was on the receiving end of Doman’s 30-yard completion on the fake punt. Buffalo Bills defensive snap counts (57 snaps) Buffalo’s defense held the Dolphins to 185 total yards, 10 first downs and three field goals. Miami quarterback Kyle McCord completed just 12 of 33 pass attempts for 102 yards and an interception, finishing with a passer rating of 32.6. The Bills accomplished all of that while distributing playing time among 24 defensive players. Defensive line and outside linebackers Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb led Buffalo’s edge rushers with 34 snaps (60%) apiece, with Rousseau accounting for both of Buffalo’s sacks. T.J. Parker played 30 snaps (53%), while Javon Solomon and Michael Hoecht played 11 (19%) and eight (14%), respectively. The interior defensive line featured a nicely balanced rotation, with Deone Walker playing 31 snaps (54%), DeWayne Carter playing 30 (53%), Greg Gaines playing 27 (47%) and Ed Oliver playing 24 (42%). Inside linebackers Shaq Thompson and Kaleb Elarms-Orr each played 31 defensive snaps (54%), while Terrel Bernard logged 29 (51%). Buffalo’s distribution of snaps at linebacker was relatively even among its three primary contributors, with just two snaps separating Thompson, Elarms-Orr and Bernard. Defensive backs Maxwell Hairston, Cole Bishop and Amani Hooker each played 46 snaps (81%), tying for the team lead. Davison Igbinosun wasn’t far behind with 44 snaps (77%). Jordan Hancock logged 26 defensive snaps (46%), while veteran cornerback Tre White played 24 (42%) and Dee Alford played 13 (23%). Sam Franklin Jr. and Jalon Kilgore contributed 12 (21%) and 11 (19%) defensive snaps, respectively, in addition to their significant special teams responsibilities. Damar Hamlin played just six defensive snaps (11%) but made the most of his limited opportunities, intercepting McCord just before halftime. Buffalo’s defensive backs helped limit Miami to just 102 passing yards. The Dolphins’ inability to sustain drives through the air was a significant factor in Buffalo’s ability to control the game. Buffalo Bills special teams snap counts (26 snaps) Sam Franklin Jr., Joe Andreessen and Javon Solomon led Buffalo’s special teams units with 19 snaps (73%) apiece, followed by Jalon Kilgore with 17 (65%) and Tyrell Shavers with 16 (62%). Michael Hoecht and Tommy Doman each logged 15 special teams snaps (58%), while Damar Hamlin played 14 (54%). Despite not recording a single punt, Doman remained heavily involved on special teams, handling kickoff and holding responsibilities in addition to executing the successful fake punt. Tyler Bass accounted for 14 of Buffalo’s 26 points, connecting on four of five field-goal attempts and both extra-point attempts. Greg Dortch and Ray Davis also contributed to Buffalo’s favorable field position in the return game. Dortch returned two kickoffs for 73 yards, while Davis added a 36-yard return. Buffalo averaged 36.3 yards per kickoff return. What’s next Buffalo’s ability to control the time of possession was a product of both the offense’s ability to sustain drives and the defense’s ability to get off the field. With just three full days between games, the ability to distribute defensive workloads without sacrificing production could prove particularly beneficial against Kansas City. If there’s one area Buffalo needs to clean up offensively before Thursday night, it’s finishing drives. The Bills generated 405 yards of offense, recorded 25 first downs and never punted, yet scored just two touchdowns. Settling for field goals against the Chiefs could prove considerably more costly than it did against the Dolphins.
author: Sara Larson

title: Bills news: Previewing the Chiefs
summary: The Buffalo Bills (9-1) host the Kansas City Chiefs (8-2) on Thanksgiving night in a battle of teams sitting at the top of their respective divisions and holding down the top two spots in the AFC. What can fans expect in Week 12, when the Bills and Chiefs meet up for the 59th time in […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills (9-1) host the Kansas City Chiefs (8-2) on Thanksgiving night in a battle of teams sitting at the top of their respective divisions and holding down the top two spots in the AFC. What can fans expect in Week 12, when the Bills and Chiefs meet up for the 59th time in a game with massive implications in the race to be the No. 1 seed in the AFC? Today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by sharing the key matchups to watch and positional analysis as Josh Allen and the Bills look to beat the Chiefs for the fifth straight time in the regular season. Check out the assessments below and then let us know your thoughts on the game in the comments section. Bills vs. Chiefs storylines to watch The Chiefs have eclipsed 34 points in their last three games, victories over the New York Jets, Atlanta Falcons, and Arizona Cardinals, while the Bills will bring a six-game winning streak into the Thanksgiving Night clash with Buffalo averaging 31 points per game during that streak. title: Week 12 Rooting interests: A Thanksgiving wish list for Bills Mafia
summary: The Buffalo Bills couldn’t have asked to start Week 12 in a better position. They’re 9-1 for the first time since 1991, have the possibility of locking up the AFC East in just two weeks, and hold the cards for the AFC’s No. 1 seed. The only thing that could make things any better would […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills couldn’t have asked to start Week 12 in a better position. They’re 9-1 for the first time since 1991, have the possibility of locking up the AFC East in just two weeks, and hold the cards for the AFC’s No. 1 seed. The only thing that could make things any better would be if the Kansas City Chiefs and Denver Broncos each had one more loss. But that’s okay. The Bills can take care of that themselves. This week is a short one, with plenty of food and football ahead. The Bills will play the nightcap of a Thanksgiving trilogy, so we don’t have much time to dissect all that could happen, but we will have plenty of postgame time to root for whatever should happen next. Here’s a look at who Bills Mafia should be watching — and rooting for (or against) — over this long weekend. _____________________________________________________________________________ AFC Standings entering Week 12 Buffalo Bills (9-1) Denver Broncos (8-2) Jacksonville Jaguars (7-3) Cincinnati Bengals (7-3) Kansas City Chiefs (8-2) Cleveland Browns (6-4) Pittsburgh Steelers (6-4) New England Patriots (5-5) Houston Texans (4-6) Las Vegas Raiders (4-7) Baltimore Ravens (4-7) New York Jets (3-8) Indianapolis Colts (3-8) Los Angeles Chargers (1-9) Miami Dolphins (1-9) Tennessee Titans (1-9) _____________________________________________________________________________ AFC EAST Kansas City Chiefs at Buffalo Bills Root for: BILLS Of course it comes down to this. Again. Bills vs. Chiefs. Josh Allen vs. Patrick Mahomes. It seems like every season, no matter what else happens, these two teams find themselves standing in each other’s way. The Bills have had the upper hand in the regular season in recent years, and we’d like to keep it that way. Thursday night’s forecast calls for cold, wet, messy football. And, quite frankly, the Bills have been playing enough messy football lately. This week, they need to be clean, even if the weather isn’t. A win would give Buffalo the head-to-head tiebreaker over one of their biggest postseason rivals, put some distance between the two teams in the AFC standings, and quiet some of the nonsense about the Bills not facing a legitimate starting quarterback over the past four weeks. This one’s for the No. 1 seed. And the bragging rights. Go Bills! New England Patriots at Los Angeles Chargers Root for: Chargers New England is coming off their bye week, and we’d love nothing more than for them to return with another loss. Two Patriot losses combined with two Bills wins would send the AFC East crown back where it belongs – Buffalo. With Buffalo heading to New England for a head-to-head matchup next week, a Chargers win this week could set the stage for the Bills to deliver the final blow to any hopes the Patriots still had of stealing a second division title. New York Jets at Miami Dolphins Root for: Dolphins Neither team is threatening Buffalo’s position in the AFC East, so we’re looking at this one a little differently. Miami has just one win, while the Jets have three. At this point, we’re more concerned with where these teams will pick in April’s NFL Draft than where they’ll finish in the division. A Miami win would give the Dolphins a little less control over the top of the draft board. And since somebody has to win this game, we’d rather it be the team with the better shot at landing the No. 1 overall pick. _____________________________________________________________________________ Rest of the AFC Denver Broncos at Pittsburgh Steelers Root for: Steelers This is probably the second most important game on the schedule this weekend – at least if you’re a Bills fan. Denver is right there in the race for the AFC’s No. 1 seed, and the Bills need someone to knock the Broncos down a notch. Pittsburgh gets its chance on Black Friday. The Steelers aren’t exactly out of the playoff picture themselves, but they’re a much smaller concern than Denver right now. And since Buffalo won’t get its own shot at the Broncos until Christmas Day, we’d be thankful if Pittsburgh could give the Bills a little help in the meantime. New Orleans Saints at Cincinnati Bengals Root for: Saints Despite Monday night’s loss to the Commanders, the Bengals are still leading the AFC North. And while Kansas City and Denver have gotten most of our attention, Cincinnati is another team Buffalo needs to keep an eye on in the race for the AFC’s top seed. Joe Burrow has quietly been leading a Bengals offense that has looked way to dangerous. If it comes down to it, I’d much rather see a January Allen-Burrow showdown happen in Buffalo than in Ohio. Baltimore Ravens at Houston Texans Root for: Ravens This one took a little more thought. Buffalo has already beaten both teams, so the head-to-head tiebreaker isn’t a concern. But which one would we rather see making a push toward the postseason? Houston is coming off a convincing win over Indianapolis, and C.J. Stroud may be starting to find his rhythm. The Texans also have a defense that causes problems for Josh Allen – definitely not want we want in January. Baltimore, meanwhile, has lost six straight and is still dealing with the absence of Lamar Jackson. If Jackson returns, the Ravens could become a much bigger threat, but first they have to find a way into the playoffs. A Baltimore win would leave both teams with losing records and make the road to January a little tougher for Houston. We’d rather see the two teams fighting to stay alive than give either one a chance to build some momentum. New York Giants at Indianapolis Colts Root for: Colts This one comes with a bit of a dilemma. Buffalo owns Indianapolis’ sixth-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft, so a Colts loss would improve the value of that selection. And since Kansas City beat Indianapolis earlier this season, another Colts loss would keep the Chiefs from getting a boost to their strength of victory. But here’s the problem. Indianapolis traded its first-round pick to the New York Jets as part of the Sauce Gardner deal, and that pick is currently projected to be No. 4 overall. So, is protecting Buffalo’s sixth-round pick and the Chiefs’ SOV tiebreaker worth helping the Jets land a potential top-three draft pick? We’re going with no. The Colts can have this one. We’d rather see the Jets picking a little later in April. Tennessee Titans at Jacksonville Jaguars Root for: Titans Jacksonville is still very much in the AFC playoff picture, and the Jaguars are another team we’d like to see fall a little further behind Buffalo. Tennessee, on the other hand, isn’t threatening anyone’s playoff position right now. There’s also that fifth-round draft pick Buffalo acquired from the Titans for 2027. We don’t want Tennessee winning too many games and hurting the value of that pick, but knocking off a potential AFC playoff contender would be worth making an exception. Las Vegas Raiders at Cleveland Browns Root for: Raiders Cleveland is still in the AFC playoff picture, even if the Browns aren’t much of a threat to Buffalo’s position at the top of the conference. A Cleveland loss would help keep some distance between the Bills and another potential postseason opponent. There’s also a strength-of-victory consideration here. Buffalo already has a win over Las Vegas, so every Raiders victory gives the Bills a little boost in that tiebreaker category. The Browns have more to lose in the standings, and the Bills have something to gain from a Raiders win. That’s enough to make this one an easy choice. _____________________________________________________________________________ NFC Rooting Interests Los Angeles Rams over Green Bay Packers – Strength of victory (SOV) Detroit Lions over Chicago Bears – Strength of victory (SOV) Minnesota Vikings over Atlanta Falcons – Strength of victory (SOV) Dallas Cowboys over Philadelphia Eagles – Keep the Jets’ 2027 first-round pick from Dallas lower in the draft. Carolina Panthers over Tampa Bay Buccaneers – Hurts Cincinnati’s SOV Arizona Cardinals over Washington…

title: Buffalo Bills chase records vs. Chiefs on Thanksgiving
summary: The Buffalo Bills have a short week, but there’s no shortage of things to watch for in our Record Book. With the Kansas City Chiefs coming to Orchard Park on Thanksgiving night, the Bills have a chance to make some history on both sides of the ball. And a win would take care of a […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills have a short week, but there’s no shortage of things to watch for in our Record Book. With the Kansas City Chiefs coming to Orchard Park on Thanksgiving night, the Bills have a chance to make some history on both sides of the ball. And a win would take care of a few entries all on its own. So, once you’ve finished your second helping of turkey and polished off that piece of pie, grab your pencils, erasers, and maybe even a permanent marker. It’s time to open up our Record Book for Week 12. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 1: Sure Things As much as we’d like to say we’re sure Josh Allen will throw a touchdown pass and James Cook III will put plenty of miles on his legs Thursday night, we’re not about to tempt fate. So, in the interest of not jinxing anyone, we’re leaving this chapter blank for Week 12. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 2: A Good Bet Greg Rousseau catches Mario Williams We got to erase a number and write in a new one for Rousseau last week as he set a new personal single-season record for sacks. This week, we’re back to looking at where he sits in Buffalo’s history books. With 42 career sacks, Rousseau is just one away from tying Mario Williams (43) for seventh on the Bills’ all-time list. Once he gets past Williams, it’ll be another Williams — Kyle (48.5) — that we’ll have our sights set on. James Cook ties an NFL record If you’ve been following along with our Record Book this season, you know the drill by now. Cook has done this in nine consecutive games, and while he’s already done something no other NFL running back has done in a single season, there’s still one more name alongside his on our watch list. Terry Allen put together a streak of 10 such games across the 1995 and 1996 seasons. If Cook can match that Thursday night, he’ll have a chance to make the record his own when the Bills head to New England next week. Josh Allen climbs the NFL’s all-time rushing touchdown list Allen had an opportunity to get this one off our list Sunday but opted to give the ball to Cook instead. The quarterback doesn’t seem to be in any hurry to add to his 90 career rushing touchdowns, which currently have him tied with Eric Dickerson and Curtis Martin. However, with the Chiefs in town Thursday night, getting into the end zone will be far more important than who gets there. Should it be Allen, he’ll move past a pair of Hall of Fame running backs and tie two more in Jerome Bettis and Franco Harris (91) for 12th on the NFL’s all-time list. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 3: Not Impossible Buffalo’s defense outlasts the 2019 Patriots The Bills have gone 43 consecutive defensive drives without allowing a touchdown, something no other Buffalo defense has ever done. Now we’re looking beyond the franchise’s Record Book. The 2019 New England Patriots went 44 consecutive drives without giving up a touchdown, and no team has put together a longer streak in a single season since. We could be getting our erasers out pretty early Thursday night. If the Bills can keep the Chiefs out of the end zone on their first two possessions, they’ll have done something no NFL defense has done in at least seven years. Dawson Knox moves up the Bills’ receiving touchdown list Knox has been hanging out in this chapter of our Record Book for a while now, but maybe this is the week we get to move him out of it. The tight end is still sitting at 28 career receiving touchdowns, tied with former Bills wide receivers Stevie Johnson and Gabe Davis. One more trip to the end zone will move him past those two and into a tie with yet another former Buffalo wide receiver, Jerry Butler (29). Josh Allen catches Jim Kelly We’ve been counting down to this one for a while now, and we’re finally at a point where it could happen on any given game day. Allen needs three passing touchdowns to tie Jim Kelly (237) for the most in Buffalo Bills history. In doing so, he’d also join Kelly at 36th on the NFL’s all-time list. Of course, we know three touchdown passes in a game isn’t asking too much of Allen. And wouldn’t it be something to see him catch Kelly in front of a national audience on Thanksgiving night? Ed Oliver climbs Buffalo’s all-time sacks list There’s something about playing football on Thanksgiving that seems to agree with Oliver. In his two previous Thanksgiving games, the defensive tackle has recorded three sacks, two forced fumbles, a fumble recovery, a safety, and 10 tackles. We only need one sack from Oliver this Thanksgiving to move him into a tie with former Bills defensive tackle Jeff Wright (31.5) for 13th in franchise history. If he has another multi-sack Thanksgiving performance, we’ll be getting the eraser out again. Tyler Bass matches a career best Bass has already made 24 field goals this season, just four shy of his single-season career high of 28. With seven games left on Buffalo’s schedule, it’s a number we could be rewriting a few times before the season is over. Whether Bass gets to 28 Thursday night probably has more to do with what the Bills’ offense does than what the kicker himself does. We certainly aren’t rooting for four Buffalo drives to stall in field-goal range, but if they do, at least there’s a little something for our Record Book. _____________________________________________________________________________ Chapter 4: Superhuman Josh Allen rewrites Buffalo’s passing touchdown record If we’re getting our pencils out for Allen in Chapter 3, we might as well keep the eraser handy. After all, if he throws three touchdown passes Thursday night, we’re going to be just one away from writing Allen’s name in place of Jim Kelly’s atop Buffalo’s all-time passing touchdown list. Kelly’s record of 237 has stood for 30 years, and while we know it’s only a matter of time before Allen takes ownership of it, four touchdown passes against the Chiefs would certainly be something to be thankful for. Buffalo’s defense keeps the Chiefs out of the end zone We’ve already talked about what the Bills could accomplish on Kansas City’s first two possessions, but what if they keep it going for all four quarters? Buffalo hasn’t allowed a touchdown in three consecutive games, and a fourth would put the Bills within one game of matching the five-game streaks put together by the 1976 Pittsburgh Steelers and the 2000 Baltimore Ravens. For a fan base — and a league — that spends so much time keeping track of what Josh Allen is doing to the record books, there’s plenty to be thankful for on the other side of the ball this year. Just five weeks ago, we were talking about a defense that ranked near the bottom of the league. Now we’re talking about whether that same defense can go an entire month without allowing a touchdown. _____________________________________________________________________________ Closing chapter: Just win We can put all of our pencils and erasers down for this one until the final whistle Thursday night. A win over the Chiefs would take care of three entries in our Record Book. At 10-1, the Bills would match the best 11-game start in franchise history, joining the 1964, 1988, and 1991 teams. And here’s a little something to think about: All three of those teams played for either a conference or league championship. A win would also give Josh Allen 98 regular-season wins, tying Russell Wilson for the most by a starting quarterback in his first nine NFL seasons. Allen would still have six games left in his ninth season to make that record his own. And then there’s Joe Brady. With a win Thursday night, Brady would have won 10 of his first 11 games as an NFL head coach — something neither Jim Harbaugh nor Kevin O’Connell did in their impressive rookie coaching seasons. As much fun as we have updating our Record Book each week, if the only entries we get to make Thursday night are the three in this…

title: Unique element of Chiefs offensive line will be vital for Buffalo Bills to exploit on Thanksgiving
summary: I have a good source on what the Chiefs offensive scheme asks of its blockers — Mitch Morse, who manned the center position in Andy Reid’s offense from 2015 – 2018. Morse is my co-host on the Buffalo Bills Radio Network pre/half/post game shows. I’ve learned a ridiculous amount about NFL blocking schemes — both […]
full_text: I have a good source on what the Chiefs offensive scheme asks of its blockers — Mitch Morse, who manned the center position in Andy Reid’s offense from 2015 – 2018. Morse is my co-host on the Buffalo Bills Radio Network pre/half/post game shows. I’ve learned a ridiculous amount about NFL blocking schemes — both run and pass — over the past three months. It’s been awesome, and I can’t express here how thankful I am for the opportunity to gain knowledge directly from someone who played his position at a high level for a long time in the NFL. And entering this seismic showdown between the Bills and Chiefs, he’s mentioned something fascinating to me — the Chiefs ask a lot of their offensive tackles. To paraphrase his analysis, Reid’s blocking unit consists of essentially two parts… a congealed three-man interior, that operates close together, as essentially as its own unit, and the two tackles out on their own respective islands. Of course, the advanced metrics validate Morse’s recollection of how Kansas City’s offensive line is structured. Below you will see “Island Rate” on the X axis, which is exactly what you’d expect — how frequently a blocker was left in a true one-on-one situation. The Y axis is pressure rate, which is also self-explanatory. Check where the Chiefs tackles reside entering this Week 12 game in Orchard Park. And three of them qualify as some injuries have hit the position this season: Benson is an undrafted rookie from Indiana, and he’s been Kansas City’s starting left tackle all season. Josh Ezeudu is the swing tackle who played 72 snaps at right tackle in Week 11’s win over the Cardinals with Jaylon Moore sidelined with an ankle injury. If Moore can practice in some capacity before Thursday, he’ll probably take over the right tackle spot on the Chiefs offensive front. They’re all being asked to block an island at a higher rate than Dion Dawkins and Spencer Brown this season, and only Moore is close to — and slightly below — league average in Island Rate. Ezeudu’s 68.3% Island Rate figure is the seventh-highest among qualifying offensive tackles to date, and Benson is tied for the third-highest Island Rate amongst this large group. Now let’s see how the Bills primary edge rushers — Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb — have fared rushing the passer when not facing double teams: Unsurprisingly, Rousseau is near the top of the NFL in pressure rate (17.8%) and has been doubled slightly more frequently than NFL average (36.6%). Chubb has a noticeably lower pressure rate (11.1%) and has dealt with doubles close to the same rate at his teammate (35.6%). As for other Bills edge rushers who don’t have enough snaps to qualify here — T.J. Parker sits with a 10.2% pressure rate and 30.7% double-team rate, Javon Solomon is at 17.1% (!) and 37.1%, and Michael Hoecht’s figures are 8.0% and 53.6%. Pay close attention to Buffalo’s edge rushers and Kansas City’s offensive tackles in this one. You’ll witness more one-on-one battles than usual, and they’re likely to be a decently sizable determining factor in this Bills-Chiefs game.

full_text: Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills and Kansas City Chiefs are set to battle in a primetime nightcap that should carry all the drama of an NFL playoff game. For football fans, it’s the perfect way to close out the Thanksgiving holiday, a matchup that’s certain to feel and play out more like a playoff game. That’s always a given when Josh Allen and Patrick Mahomes rekindle their friendship. At 9-1, the Bills remain in first place in the AFC, and in control of their playoff destiny. The Chiefs, at 8-2, are hot on their tails. A slip-up by Buffalo would open the door for the Chiefs to take over first place and potentially secure homefield advantage throughout the playoffs. So while this may just be a regular-season affair, the outcome of Thursday’s game will reverberate well into the postseason. Since the Allen vs. Mahomes rivalry began, their teams have a 5-5 head-to-head record. It’s a series that favors the Bills in the regular season, and the Chiefs in the postseason. In fact, Buffalo has won only two of the seven postseason games against Kansas City, and the team has gone 0-4 since the playoffs for the 2020 NFL season. There’s perhaps no bigger spotlight than an NFL game in primetime during the holidays, when most of the country and much of the world gather with loved ones to share their love of the game. title: Panthers vs Ravens game review: One to remember
summary: There are some games that you forgot moments after turning off the TV. Nothing overly notable happens, the game starts, some stuff happens, then the game ends and you move on with your day. Other days, you’re treated to something else. Something so clearly special that you know it will forever be revered within the […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - NOVEMBER 22: Carolina Panthers safety Tre'von Moehrig (7) punches the ball loose from Baltimore Ravens running back Justice Hill (43) causing a touch back during an NFL football game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Carolina Panthers on November 22, 2026 at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. (Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images There are some games that you forgot moments after turning off the TV. Nothing overly notable happens, the game starts, some stuff happens, then the game ends and you move on with your day. Other days, you’re treated to something else. Something so clearly special that you know it will forever be revered within the annals of your team’s fandom. Sunday’s folly-fueled masterpiece versus the Baltimore Ravens was one of those such games. This is a moment in history, a game not to be forgotten, and for this week’s game review we are creating a time capsule to forever remember the moments that made this game the experience that it was. We should have known what we were in for once news broke late in the week that Ravens cornerback Marlon Humphrey was not going to play. Not due to injury or even on-field performance, but simply from being terrible in front of a microphone. Humphrey crossed a line with comments made on his personal podcast and the team decided to make him inactive for at least the game versus the Panthers. Starting off 2-0 (1st Quarter, 12:22 remaining, score 0-2) There’s something visually wrong about an NFL score being 2-0. After forcing a 3 and out on the first drive, Trevor Etienne elects not to fair catch the punt that eventually gets downed inside the 5-yard. A bad situation gets worse as Bryce Young chooses the absolute worse time to try and show he can actually stand tall in the pocket. He holds onto it for a hair too long and is brought down for a safety. MIKE GREEN GETS THE SAFETY TO START THE GAME!!! Tune in on FOX! pic.twitter.com/P9ELR2vDru — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) November 22, 2026 Ravens get tricky (1st Quarter, 11:21 remaining, score 0-9) On the ensuing drive after receiving the post-safety kickoff, the Ravens decided the start to the game wasn’t embarrassing enough so far for the Panthers. Cue the wildcat formation double pass 52 yard touchdown pass. Brissett finds Bateman deep for the TD! 📺: FOX/FOX One pic.twitter.com/1TyvYFDaT7 — FOX Sports: NFL (@NFLonFOX) November 22, 2026 Is that you, J-Stew? (1st Quarter, 12:22 remaining, score 0-12) On the first play of the drive following a Ravens field goal, Chuba Hubbard channels his inner Jonathan Stewart to stiff arm Ravens All-Pro safety Kyle Hamilton into the turf and bring some life to the Panthers sideline. Stay out of Chuba Hubbard’s way 😤 @Panthers | @NFLCanada pic.twitter.com/KmxgcQPZdS — NFL (@NFL) November 23, 2026 Panthers get trickier (1st Quarter, 0:01 remaining, score 7-12) Not to be outdone in their own stadium, the Panthers deploy a trick play of their own to great effect. A direct snap to Jalen Coker, who flips the ball back to Young, who sends a dime to wide open Mitchell Evans, who crosses the goal line a moment later. Mitch gets us on the board 😤 #BALvsCAR 📺 FOX pic.twitter.com/Xe2XykUoOB — Carolina Panthers (@Panthers) November 22, 2026 The best rule in football (2nd Quarter, 12:17 remaining, score 7-12) Following the Panthers touchdown, the Ravens respond by marching 41 yards in 4 plays before Ravens running back Justice Hill breaks off for a 36 yard scamper that includes a stiff arm to Will Lee for the last 10 yards or so. What it didn’t include the entire time, however, was the football as Lee managed swat the ball out of Hill’s possession just before crossing the goal line. It rolled through the back of the endzone for a touchback. What a play by Will Lee III near the goal line BALvsCAR on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/3YDivudKpP — NFL (@NFL) November 22, 2026 Ravens go full Panther (2nd Quarter, 10:47 remaining, score 7-12) Even though Lee’s goal line heroics kept the score from becoming 7-19, the game still seemed bleak. Unable to do anything with the gifted possession, the Panthers go 3 and out. The ensuing punt, however, doinks off Ravens punt returner LaJohntay Wester before Brycen Tremayne jumps on top of it. 2 plays later Hubbard is crossing the goal line on a nifty 18 yard run. Muffed punt and the Panthers get it back! BALvsCAR on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/v00xqwNRgA — NFL (@NFL) November 22, 2026 The wheels officially come off (2nd Quarter, 9:49 remaining, score 14-19) Things were looking up for the Panthers after Hubbard scored to put them ahead 14-12. That lasted for precisely 12 seconds, which is how long it took Ravens kick returner Tez Walker to return the following kickoff 86 yards. Panthers Special Teamer Malcolm DeWalt lost Walker on a spin move and it was off to the races from there. THE TARHEEL TEZ BACK IN CAROLINA WITH THE KICK RETURN TUDDY!!! TUNE IN ON FOX! pic.twitter.com/WdrKLHgEpM — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) November 22, 2026 2 point conversion? Don’t mind if I do. (2nd Quarter, 5:06 remaining, score 22-19) The Panthers offense comes to life following the delating kick return touchdown. A 9 play, 69 yard drive that ends with Young finding Tetairoa McMillan in the back of the endzone. After Fitzgerald puts the extra point through, the Panthers lead 21-19. That is until the yellow flag comes out and an unnecessary roughness penalty is called on the Ravens. Panthers accept and are given the ball at the 1 yard line where Hubbard converts from a moment later. Never go full Joe Adams (2nd Quarter, 1:15 remaining, score 22-26) What’s funnier than one muffed punt? Two muffed punts. It’s probably not funny if you’re Wester, who took a page out of infamous Panthers punt returner Joe Adams and decided that catching punts is not in his job descriptions. Unfortunately, DeWalt was unable to accept the generous gift and the Ravens eventually recovered within their own 5 yard line. Players gotta start putting in their mouthguard 😭 pic.twitter.com/kE43MxjpU6 — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 22, 2026 “Why???” we all screamed in unison (3rd Quarter, 5:44 remaining, score 29-26) An encouraging beginning to the 2nd half where the Panthers once again took the lead with the first drive of the quarter, forced a 3 and out, and find themselves driving down the field and facing 3rd and goal from the 3. What followed was a scramble drill to the right right where Young makes the incomprehensible decision to attempt a throw to McMillan in the back of the endzone. The ball was behind McMillan and Ravens corner TJ Tampa finishes the play with the ball in his hands. A devastating turnover when trying to put the game out of reach. TJ Tampa diving INT in the end zone! BALvsCAR on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/y6fHFuDJUI — NFL (@NFL) November 22, 2026 Welcome to the NFL (4th Quarter, 15:00 remaining, score 29-26) The first play of the 4th quarter will be a memorable one for Raven’s rookie Vega Ioane, the 14th overall pick. Safety Tre’Von Moehrig came flying in with violence to meet the 320lb pulling guard. At about a 100lb disadvantage, the 215lb safety sent the lineman flying backwards. My goodness 🧱 pic.twitter.com/WrlerC4OOb — NFL (@NFL) November 22, 2026 Will Lee, you have my attention (4th Quarter, 14:23 remaining, score 29-26) After tightening up in the 3rd quarter, the Ravens have the ball again as the final quarter begins. A pass on 1st and 15 is punched out of Henry’s hands by Lee to fall incomplete. At least, that’s what it looked like until Dave Canales threw the little red flag on the ground to have them take another look. Turns out that Henry took one too many steps with the ball in his hands. The catch counted, and thus so did the now-fumble that Tyrel Dodson had recovered. Panthers ball. Aggies Helping Aggies Will Lee forced the fumble & Tyrel Dodson scoops it up.…

title: NFL Predictions: Bears will get their first win in Detroit since 2021
summary: Thursday is the biggest regular-season game between the Chicago Bears and the Detroit Lions in a really long time. The Athletic’s Kevin Fishbain dug up that the only two years both the Bears and Lions made the playoffs were 1994 and 1991. With each team currently holding a 90% chance to make the postseason, the […]
full_text: Sep 14, 2025; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson and Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell hug after the game at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: Lon Horwedel-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Thursday is the biggest regular-season game between the Chicago Bears and the Detroit Lions in a really long time. The Athletic’s Kevin Fishbain dug up that the only two years both the Bears and Lions made the playoffs were 1994 and 1991. With each team currently holding a 90% chance to make the postseason, the odds are pretty good that it happens again. In 1994, both teams snuck into the playoffs at 9-7, but in 1991 the Lions won the NFC Central at 12-4, with the Bears right behind at 11-5. They split the series in ’91, with the Bears winning at Soldier Field and the Lions winning ugly at the Pontiac Silverdome on Thanksgiving, 16-6. The winner of this Thanksgiving Day game will move to 9-2, be the two-seed in the NFC, and claim the top spot in the division with just six games to go. Our partners at FanDuel Sportsbook have the Bears as a 1.5-point favorite (it opened at 2.5, so money has been coming in on the Lions) with the over/under at 55.5, which is the highest point total this week. I went back and forth on my prediction all week, and I can see it going either way, but give me the Bears to win, 28 to 27. So that’s the Bears and the moneyline (-122), the Lions and the 1.5 points (-112), and the under (-112). Not only is Ben Johnson looking for his first win over the Lions, but Caleb Williams is too. The last time the Bears beat Detroit, Justin Fields had 289 combined yards, Chicago sacked Jared Goff 4 times, and he had 3 turnovers. The last time the Bears won in Detroit, Andy Dalton threw for 317 yards, with Darnell Mooney catching 5 for 123. Did you realize the Lions are just 1-8 on Thanksgiving since 2017? The Bears are 3-1 against them on Turkey Day in that stretch, with the only loss coming in 2024 when Matt Eberflus was a deer in headlights in the waning seconds, forgetting to call a timeout, and was fired the next day. title: Caleb Williams Week 11 QB Grade: Bears vs Saints Film Breakdown
summary: A Quick Note: Due to holiday travel plans I won’t be doing in-depth breakdown with individual plays, we will return to those for Week 12! Coming off the bye, I think many of us expected a little more fireworks from the Bears offense against New Orleans. Instead, Chicago started slowly, put together consecutive touchdown drives […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - NOVEMBER 22: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears is pressured in the pocket during the second quarter against the New Orleans Saints at Soldier Field on November 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images A Quick Note: Due to holiday travel plans I won’t be doing in-depth breakdown with individual plays, we will return to those for Week 12! Coming off the bye, I think many of us expected a little more fireworks from the Bears offense against New Orleans. Instead, Chicago started slowly, put together consecutive touchdown drives to open up a 16-0 lead, and largely managed the game from there in a 21-13 win. It wasn’t particularly pretty, but the Bears improved to 8-2 with their fifth straight victory. Caleb Williams capitalized on both of the defense’s second-quarter takeaways, finding D’Andre Swift on a 3-yard shovel pass before connecting with Colston Loveland for a 15-yard touchdown. Loveland supplied the highlight with a hurdle over Julian Blackmon, while Williams helped turn those extra possessions into some breathing room. Williams finished 15 of 23 for 181 yards, two touchdowns and one interception on a deflected pass. There were opportunities left on the field, but I think the context of what he was being asked to do matters quite a bit this week. My charting had Williams attempting a pass from under center on just four of 28 dropbacks , a 14.3% rate compared with his season mark of 32.8%. That’s an 18.5-percentage-point drop, and a noticeable departure from Chicago’s usual approach. The formation and personnel numbers added another layer . Chicago used at least three receivers aligned wide on 15 of those 28 dropbacks, while 19 came in 11 personnel. That 67.9% dropback rate stands out alongside the Bears’ 49.4% overall season usage, although those aren’t identical samples. I don’t have a seasonal baseline for the wide alignments, so that number is descriptive rather than proof of an increase. Fellow WCG writer Lester Wiltfong Jr. came away with a similar impression of the simplified game plan . With Detroit waiting on Thanksgiving, it wouldn’t surprise me if Johnson kept some things close to the chest. That’s my read, though, rather than something these numbers can establish. StartKyleOrton pointed out that Chicago ran the ball 20 times on first down, with just four classified as successful . That’s useful context when evaluating Williams, because an ineffective running game can make the passing game’s job considerably harder. I can see the argument that Johnson wanted to work through some of those issues, but whatever his intent, the offense’s overall production and Caleb’s individual performance deserve separate consideration. None of that gives the offense a free pass. New Orleans cut the lead to 16-10 before halftime, and Chicago needed a third-quarter field goal to restore a two-possession cushion. Still, with the defense producing six sacks and Montez Sweat adding a fourth-quarter safety, Williams didn’t have to carry this one. It was a workmanlike win with plenty to clean up before Thursday. With the short turnaround, let’s get right into the benchmarks. Benchmarks (Season totals are underlined , Season Averages in Italics , and this week’s stats appear in regular text.) C/A: 134/195 (68.7%) | 22.3/32.5 (68.7%) | 15/23 (65.2%) Yards: 1546 | 25 6 | 181 Touchdowns: 10 | 1.7 | 2 Turnovers: 5 | 0.8 | 1 QB at Fault Sacks: 1 | 0.2 | 2 aDOT: 7.7 | 10.9 Passer Rating: 95.4 | 100.1 True Passer Rating : 115.7 | 139.7 Time to Throw: 3.10s | 2.84s Time to Pressure: 2.55s | 2.55s Pressure Rate: 37.05% | 34.482% On-Target Rate: 85.9% | 68.4% Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 5.6 % PPR / 8.8% BRP | 0.0% PPR / 12.9% BRP EPA per dropback: +0. 15 | -0.01 ANY/A : 6.6 | 6.4 Game Scorecard The full grading sheet for each play can be found here. Game Notes NFL Passer Rating / True Passer Rating / PFN Impact Score: 100.1 / 139.7 / 76.7 The NFL’s average passer rating through Week 11 sits at 91.3, putting Williams’ 100.1 comfortably above that mark and 11th among qualifying quarterbacks this week. His two touchdown passes helped offset the interception, producing a respectable result despite the offense’s uneven afternoon. His ability to remain efficient with a 7.9 yards per attempt also helped keep his passer rating healthy. This is where the box score and the individual grading can tell slightly different stories. Williams finished with a good passer rating, but that doesn’t mean his accuracy or execution was consistently where we’d like it to be (or where we’ve seen it for the most part of the year.) A 139.7 TPR represents a “Great” outing, matching the mark Williams posted against Seattle in Week 8. That result adds some perspective to an uneven afternoon. His accuracy wasn’t as consistent as we’d like, particularly underneath, but the quality of his better plays still deserves recognition, hitting on 5 of his 7 throws beyond 10 yards and posting a season high 10.9 aDOT also helps. On the PFN scale, where 75 represents an average qualifying starter and 90 is elite territory, Williams finished Week 11 with a 76.7 Impact Score, ranking 10th among 26 qualifying quarterbacks. That’s a slightly above-average result and a reasonable reflection of the afternoon overall. Williams contributed to the win, but this wasn’t a performance that required him to carry the offense or consistently overcome difficult circumstances. On-Target Throws: 2026 Average: 85.9% | Week 11: 68.4% Reminder: Completion percentage ≠ On-Target Percentage. I only chart aimed passes, meaning throwaways, spikes and passes deflected at the line are excluded. Drops can still be credited as on-target. Short-Level Passing (Behind LOS–9 yards): 8/12 | 66.7% On-Target Deep-Level Passing (10+ Yards Downfield): 5/7 | 71.4% On-Target This was the most disappointing part of Williams’ afternoon for me. He finished on target on just 13 of 19 aimed throws, putting him 17.5 percentage points below his season mark. And while the misses we’re say at the level we saw in early 2025, it was an uncharacteristic outing in the context of 2026. The short-level accuracy stands out in particular. Four off-target throws on 12 attempts underneath is a considerable amount of missed execution in an area where we’ve seen greater consistency in 2026. Worth noting, 2 of those 4 off-target throws were still caught, they just required beyond ordinary effort relative to the throw difficulty. Williams was actually more accurate on throws traveling at least 10 yards downfield, although seven attempts is a small sample. The takeaway isn’t that the deeper passing was flawless, but that the shorter throws weren’t providing the dependable efficiency this offense needed. Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 0.0% PPR / 12.9% BPR Williams finished without a “Poor” graded play while still producing a 12.9% Big Play Rate. That combination helps explain how he earned a “Good” final grade despite the accuracy issues. An off-target throw doesn’t automatically qualify as a “Poor” play in my grading. Accuracy, decision-making, difficulty and the circumstances of the play all matter, so the lower on-target percentage and clean Poor Play Rate aren’t contradictory. His interception goes “Ungraded” because it came on a pass deflected at the line of scrimmage. Under my grading approach, I don’t assign quarterback blame for the unpredictable outcome of those deflections, and in most cases a defensive lineman leaving his feet is the fault of the offensive line. That doesn’t erase the turnover or its impact on the game. It means I’m separating the result of the play from what I’m assigning to Williams individually. EPA per Dropback: 2026 Average: +0.15 | Week 11: -0.01 Williams finished just below neutral at -0.01 EPA per dropback, a noticeable step down from his +0.15 season average. There were productive moments, but the passing game didn’t generate sustained efficiency across the…
