title: Detroit Lions vs. Chicago Bears preview, prediction: On Paper
summary: The 8-2 Detroit Lions face the 8-2 Chicago Bears face off on Thursday for one of the most anticipated Thanksgiving Day matchups in recent history. The NFC North lead is on the line, but which team holds the advantage? Let’s take a closer look in our Lions vs. Bears preview and prediction: On Paper. Lions […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - SEPTEMBER 14: Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions looks on at the line of scrimmage against the Chicago Bears at Ford Field on September 14, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 8-2 Detroit Lions face the 8-2 Chicago Bears face off on Thursday for one of the most anticipated Thanksgiving Day matchups in recent history. The NFC North lead is on the line, but which team holds the advantage? Let’s take a closer look in our Lions vs. Bears preview and prediction: On Paper. Lions pass offense (8th in DVOA) vs. Bears pass defense (10th) My season-long faith in the Lions’ passing attack was awarded last week when I gave Detroit the advantage despite the Bucs’ pass defense (3rd) ranking significantly higher than Detroit’s (11th) in DVOA. Based on all the evidence, I still believe DVOA hasn’t caught up to Detroit’s true efficiency through the air, although they are getting closer now. For the season, Detroit’s passing attack ranks: Fourth in passer rating (107.8) Fourth in yards per attempt (8.2) Third in dropback EPA (0.217) Third in dropback success rate (52.5%) By nearly all accounts, this is a top-five passing attack, and it feels like the only time they’ve really been slowed down is a weird game against the Dolphins (I blame Christian Mahogany’s benching) and against the unique Vikings defense. Last week’s dominance against the Buccaneers only strengthened my resolve that this unit is nearly unstoppable, and they may be getting better. Pass protection is pretty darn solid, and that’s going to be important this week against a surging Bears defensive line. Detroit ranks fourth in ESPN’s pass block win rate, second in PFF pass blocking grade, and ninth in pressure rate allowed. The Bears’ pass defense has been pretty up and down this year, but my eye is immediately drawn to the last three games. They’ve shut down the Seahawks, Bucs, and Saints—admittedly not great passing offenses—but it’s hard not to connect that with the recent addition of Jeffery Simmons, who has been an absolute monster in the last three games. In his short time with the Bears, he already has five sacks and two pass breakups. But the Lions’ offensive line and passing attack will be Chicago’s biggest defensive test they’ve faced since at least the Patriots—maybe all season. Chicago’s season-long averages are good but not great: 17th in passer rating allowed (89.8) 25th in yards per attempt (7.7) Seventh in dropback EPA (-0.036) Fifth in dropback success rate (41.9%) It’s an odd split of stats, seeing them so pedestrian in basic statistics, but nearly elite in advanced stats. I think there are two reasons for this disconnect. One, I think Chicago may be giving up a fair amount of garbage time stats. When we only account for data when the win percentage is between 5-95% (a very small cutting out of garbage time stats), Chicago’s pass defense jumps to second in EPA and second in success rate. Additionally, the Bears create a ton of disruptive plays. Again, they are near the top of the league in interception (eight, t-10th), and they’re also fourth in sacks (32). But if you can pass protect and take care of the ball, there is some vulnerability here. The Lions are pretty darn good at doing both of those things. Player to watch: Simmons. I don’t think you can overstate his impact on the game. It’s not just Simmons being unstoppable, but he’s made his surrounding cast much better. Montez Sweat has 12 pressures in three games since Simmons was back, Grady Jarrett has nine, and Austin Booker has 11. Advantage: Lions +1.5. The Bears believe they can create pressure with just four players now, which has helped a struggling secondary. I’m not so sure Chicago can get away with that this week. They’ll create some issues, and it’ll be important for Jared Goff to take care of the football. However, it feels like the Lions have answers for everything the Bears do well in this matchup. Lions run offense (1st) vs. Bears run defense (18th) Detroit’s running game wasn’t flashy against the Buccaneers, but it was effective. The Lions were able to consistently stay ahead of the sticks despite going up against the best run defense in football, and eventually they broke through with a few explosives late in the game to seal the win. That performance should give you confidence the Lions can run against just about anybody. It really feels like they’ve found answers since that Vikings game. For the year, Detroit ranks: Ninth in yards per carry (4.5) Eighth in rush EPA (0.003) Third in success rate (49.6%) And since that Vikings game? Seventh in yards per carry (4.9) Fourth in rush EPA (0.106) Third in success rate (51.1%) And mind you in those four weeks, the Lions have faced two of the best run defenses in football (Vikings and Bucs). All of that is to say I’m pretty darn confident in this rushing attack right now. The offensive line is coming together, as evidenced by their rank in adjusted line yards (second), run-block win rate (fourth), and PFF run-block grade (fourth). It’s hard to get a handle on the Bears’ run defense because they haven’t faced a lot of runs this season. Because they haven’t been trailing in a game since October 11, Chicago has faced a league-low 207 attempts (next lowest is 230). But in terms of down-to-down efficiency, they actually aren’t that good. They rank: 25th in yards per carry allowed (4.5) 12th in rush EPA (-0.064) 14th in rush success rate (41.2%) But there is something that they do really excel at and that’s short-yardage situations. They’re allowing conversions on just 47% of those situations, which is the second-best mark in the NFL. That’s something the Lions struggled with early in the season, but have improved at significantly as of late. For the year, Detroit is now converting on 74% of power runs, sixth-highest. Digging deeper, I’m not all that impressed by the Bears’ statistical marks. They’re 27th in run-stop win rate, 31st in PFF run-defense grade, and 18th in adjusted line yards. Simmons certainly helps, but this feels like a weakness that Chicago has been able to hide well because of game script. Player to watch: Austin Booker. The third-year Bears defensive end is having a solid season, and his 76.8 run-defense grade is ninth-best among edge defenders. But he mostly lines up opposite the left tackle. So we’ll see how he fares against Penei Sewell. Advantage: Lions +2. My confidence has never been higher in the Lions’ run game, and while Chicago hasn’t allowed more than 126 rushing yards in a game, I think that’s a mirage caused by facing mostly poor rushing attacks and forcing teams to abandon the run game by getting out to early leads. Bears pass offense (12th) vs. Lions pass defense (21st) Bold and italicized data indicate games in which Caleb Williams was out There’s been ups and downs in Caleb Williams’ third NFL season, but far more ups than downs. Let’s compare his statline from last year to this year: 2025: 58.1% completion percentage, 6.9 Y/A, 27 TDs, 7 INTs, 90.1 passer rating 2026: 68.3% completion percentage, 7.9 Y/A, 10 TDs, 6 INTs, 95.9 passer rating He’s been more accurate, deadlier down the field, and while the interceptions are up, that’s largely the result of a single four-interception outing against the Bucs. For the season, the Bears rank: 19th in passer rating (88.8) 14th in yards per attempt (7.4) 13th in dropback EPA (0.089) Sixth in success rate (51.5%) Another big difference between 2025 and 2026 Williams is the deep shot. Last year, he was uncorking a deep shot 10.6% of the time. That’s down to just 8.3% this year, as he’s learned to better take what the defense is giving him. His average depth of target is slightly down, too, dropping from 8.5 to 8.2. Some of the mediocre stats are the result of a three-game stretch without Williams. But there are some underlying issues, too. Most notably, the pass protection has taken a small step back from last year. But where the passing…

We had the pleasure of connecting with Bill Zimmerman, Deputy Editor of Windy City Gridiron, to give us some insight into this […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - JANUARY 04: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears scrambles to throw while pressured by Rock Ya-Sin #23 of the Detroit Lions in the second quarter at Soldier Field on January 04, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s a Thanksgiving Day matchup that no one will soon forget: the Detroit Lions (8-2) will take on the Chicago Bears (8-2) from Ford Field for the sole spot atop the NFC North. We had the pleasure of connecting with Bill Zimmerman, Deputy Editor of Windy City Gridiron, to give us some insight into this Chicago squad ahead of Thursday afternoon’s divisional tilt. We learned about Caleb Williams’ Year 3 leap into the top-10 quarterback conversation, what’s behind the sudden regression of Chicago’s rushing attack, and how injuries in the secondary have forced Dennis Allen into heavier base looks—plus how trade-deadline acquisition Jeffery Simmons has transformed the Bears’ defensive front into a top-10 unit. 1. Last week, Mike Florio and Chris Simms talked about Caleb Williams’ chances at being the league’s MVP , with Florio claiming Williams “would be one of the top MVP candidates right now if he hadn’t missed those three games,” and Simms stating that Caleb has “injected himself into the conversation of the best quarterback in the NFL.” Do you agree with these bold proclamations? If so, where in Williams’ game have you seen him make the leap to becoming an elite quarterback? In what areas do you think he still has room to grow in Year 3? Alright, so let’s play this out. Caleb never gets hurt. What is the Bears record? There’s a good chance they win the game against Minnesota. Caleb was literally going in for the go ahead score when he hurt his hamstring. What would have happened against Green Bay? Hard to say, but let’s say they lose that game in a far more competitive football game. If the Bears are 9-1 right now with Caleb doing some of the things he’s done on national television, I do think he would be in the MVP conversation. However, if I’m being fully objective, 4 interceptions on Sunday Night Football followed up by a subpar performance against the New Orleans Saints would have derailed any hope he would have at the MVP in 2026. That being said, I do think Caleb has taken significant strides and is playing outstanding football. Since he’s returned from injury, the Bears have literally not trailed for 1 second in a football game. That’s since October 11 th . Caleb hasn’t trailed in a football game since September 20 th . He’s operating in structure very well, his completion percentage (what everyone loved to complain about last year) is now 3 rd in the league, and he still has the ability to make absurd throws on the move with incredible accuracy and velocity on the football. So do I think Caleb is an MVP candidate, even if he was healthy? No. But I do think Caleb is pushing to be one of the top 5 QBs in the league and could get there if he plays well down the stretch against strong competition. I think he should be considered one of the top 10 QBs in the league right now. 2. Chicago’s run game was one of their biggest strengths a year ago, ranking fourth in EPA/rush and second in rush success rate. This season, the Bears rank 17th in EPA/rush and 16th in rush success rate. How much of that slide back to being an average rushing attack has to do with Kyle Monangai’s extended absence? D’Andre Swift is averaging just 3.7 yards per carry, down from 4.9 yards per carry a season ago, and his success rate this year (48.8%) has taken a hit as well, down from 54.7% in 2025. How much of this is on the running backs, how much of this has to do with the offensive line, and how much of it has had to do with matchups or quality of opponent? Your guess on the run game is as good as mine, and honestly, maybe Ben Johnson. The running game has not been nearly as strong this year even though it’s still a point of emphasis. Kyle Monangai being out certainly hurt, but he was back against the Saints last week and people (Tom Brady included) were expecting a big leap forward and it didn’t happen. If the Bears are going to be a true Super Bowl contender this year, they need to figure out the running game and get it closer to the 2025 version than what it’s largely been in 2026. They’ve shown the ability to run it just as well earlier in the year, but they haven’t been firing the last few weeks. Perhaps it’s that the offensive line isn’t quite as strong this year. Darnell Wright and Jonah Jackson are still a dynamite run-blocking duo on the right side, but Joe Thuney might be showing his age, he’s still good but not elite like last season and Drew Dalman’s surprise retirement forcing them to go to Garrett Bradbury has been a significant downgrade at center. Either way, as Lions fans, you know how important the run game is to Ben Johnson and he’s still going to be focused on making sure it’s working as we go down the stretch here in the regular season. 3. Chicago’s defense has undergone some pretty dramatic changes from a year ago in terms of personnel deployment. Last year, the Bears lined up in base just 12.6% of the time, the third-lowest rate in the NFL. In 2026, the Bears find themselves in base on 33.8% of snaps, the eighth-highest clip in the league. What changes to Chicago’s roster dictated this shift to more base personnel? How much of this scheme change has helped the Bears defense improve this season, going from 19th in EPA/play to seventh? Honestly, the biggest thing that happened were injuries and issues in their secondary. The Bears planned on having a secondary of rookie Dillon Thieneman and Coby Bryant at safety and Jaylon Johnson and Tyrique Stevenson at outside corners and Kyler Gordon at nickel. Coby Bryant went down in August and hasn’t played yet, that’s forced backup Nickel Cam Lewis to play a lot of safety. Kyler Gordon also missed a ton of time as well, and the other backup nickel, rookie Malik Muhammad was already playing outside because Tyrique Stevenson has been hurt and ineffective when he’s been healthy. I think Dennis Allen has just realized that until his secondary is healthier and playing better, putting their third linebacker, D’Marco Jackson, on the field, who’s decent in coverage as is, was a better option than whatever was left in their secondary room. 4. The Bears took a huge swing at the trade deadline, acquiring Jeffery Simmons to hold things down in the middle of their defense. The pressures and the sacks were a given, but in what other ways have you noticed Simmons making an impact for Chicago’s defense that maybe you weren’t expecting? Jeffery Simmons has elevated the entire Bears defense from a liability to a top-ten unit in the league. Yes, Simmons is making an impact on the stat sheet. But how he’s elevated everyone else on the D is incredible. Montez Sweat is playing his best football since 2023. Grady Jarrett hasn’t been great since becoming a Bear last year, he’s much better. Austin Booker at the other edge is making impact plays. Devin Bush was brought in as a free agent and he’d been bogged down with blockers the first several games, but now he’s running free and making big plays. Not only that, the Bears are now getting pressure with 4 and Dennis Allen doesn’t have to blitz nearly as much so that’s more bodies to drop back in a weak secondary, and pressure is getting home quicker so they don’t have to cover as long. Not only that, but Simmons is already a leader in the locker room both vocally and by example. This is one of the great midseason acquisitions I can ever remember and probably the best one in the history of the Chicago Bears. 5. The Bears opened as 2.5-point favorites over at FanDuel Sportsbook heading into this Thanksgiving Day matchup against the Lions. What’s one thing you want to see, what’s one thing you need to see, and one thing you’re sure you’ll see happen in this matchup between the Lions and Bears on Thursday? I’ve…

title: Lions Week 12 preview: Breaking down Bears’ offensive, defensive schemes
summary: In Week 12, the Detroit Lions (8-2) and Chicago Bears (8-2) will square off in a Thanksgiving Day showdown at Ford Field, with the NFC North’s top spot on the line. For the second week in a row, Lions coach Dan Campbell is very familiar with the opponent’s coaching staff: the Bears are led by […]
full_text: Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images | Getty Images In Week 12, the Detroit Lions (8-2) and Chicago Bears (8-2) will square off in a Thanksgiving Day showdown at Ford Field, with the NFC North’s top spot on the line. For the second week in a row, Lions coach Dan Campbell is very familiar with the opponent’s coaching staff: the Bears are led by former Lions offensive coordinator Ben Johnson, along with several other former Lions coaches, and a few individuals he coached alongside in New Orleans. “Obviously got a real good opponent coming up. It’s a hot team, 8-2 like we are. A division opponent. Ben (Johnson)’s done a hell of a job out there, so has (Bears Defensive Coordinator Dennis Allen) DA. I mentioned this before, I know a lot of those coaches, obviously we had them on staff here and then a lot of coaches that I coached with at New Orleans when I was there, (Bears Offensive line coach) Dan Roushar, O-line coach, certainly DA. So, got a lot of respect for what they do out there.” Let’s take a closer look at the Bears’ coaching staff, the scheme that they run, and some scouting notes from previously viewed games. Bears head coach: Ben Johnson NFL coaching seasons: 15th season (Bears, Lions, Dolphins) Head coaching seasons: Second (Bears 2025-present) Offensive coordinator seasons : Three (Lions 2022-24) Influences: Dan Campbell, Zac Taylor, Darrell Bevell, Mike Martz, Adam Gase, Mike Sherman, Bill Lazor Coached under : Campbell, Matt Patricia, Gase, Joe Philbin Playcaller : Yes Since Bears coach Ben Johnson left the Lions for the Chicago’s head coaching job, he’s taken the league by storm, but has surprisingly struggled against the NFC North. Against non-NFC North opponents, Johnson’s Bears are 15-2, but against division rivals, Chicago is just 2-6, including losses to the Lions both times they’ve played and a 52-21 loss the last time he was in Ford Field. Expect Johnson to be motivated to change the narrative this week. Offensive coordinator: Press Taylor NFL coaching seasons : 14 seasons (Bears, Jaguars, Colts, Eagles) Offensive coordinator seasons : Fourth (Bears 2026, Jaguars 2022-24) Previous positions held : Passing game coordinator (Bears 2025, Eagles 2020), QB coach, Offensive assistant, Assistant QB coach, quality control Influences: Zac Taylor (Bengals HC, brother), Ben Johnson, Doug Pederson, Frank Reich, Chip Kelly Coached under : Johnson, Pederson, Reich, Kelly Lions ties to coaching staff : Antwaan Randle El (WR coach), J.T. Barrett (QB coach) Offensive scheme Passing game : Ben Johnson’s West Coast, Modern Pro-style scheme Running scheme : Multiple, Gap and Outside zone Staples of scheme : Primarily 11 personnel (50% on the season, 56% over last four games) They use 12 personnel more than 90% of the NFL (33% on the season, 30% over last four) 13 personnel has been scaled back a bit (16.6% season, 13% last four) but still above 80% of teams Core values: Strive for run-pass balance (55-45 split), heavy play action (36%, most in the NFL), pre-snap motion, bunch formations, YAC (9th most in NFL), screens, gadget plays, trick plays, willing to run on any down and distance, not scared to go for it on 4th down (58% success rate, 13th) Put points and yards on the board: 26.2 per game (8th); 375.8 yards per game (8th) Strive to control the ball/clock with time of possession: 56.86% (best in NFL) QB Caleb Williams is willing to hold on to the ball to try and make a big play Passing explosives in last four games: 12.7% (third best in the NFL) Passer rating is slightly above average: 95.9 (12th) Williams EPA per dropback: +0.15 (11th) Solid vs. Zone coverage (EPA: +0.11, 13th), but below average vs. Man coverage (EPA: -0.01, 26th) Teams blitz Williams at the highest rate in the NFL (49%); for good reason (EPA: -0.03, 22nd) Williams scramble skill keep pressure/sacks low: 19th in pressures, 22nd in rate; 12th in sacks and rate Rome Odunze is the deep shot receiver: EPA: 50.23; Target share: 17.5% Luther Buren is a volume/consistent receiver: EPA: 31.36; Target share: 22% TE Colston Loveland = volume/consistent: EPA: 26.82; Target share: 19% Run game is heavy outside zone (54% of runs); Outside runs 61% of the time (4th most) Run game numbers can be deceiving if you only look at the box score: 142.4 per-game average (3rd) The rest of the numbers are average at best Rush yards per attempt: 4.2 (14th); EPA per rush: -0.06 (16th) Explosive runs over last four games: 5.3% (31st in the NFL) Runs of 10+ yards: 29 on season (13th) — only six in the last four games Success rate over last four games: 40.8% (16th) Rush yards over expectations: -27 (20th) Dan Campbell on the Bears’ offense : “They’re finding ways to win. (QB) Caleb (Williams), he’s a heck of a player, man. Dynamic. And they have got weapons, man. (WR Luther) Burden’s having a big year. (TE) Colston (Loveland), the O-line’s playing well. They’ve been able to stay intact, play together. (RB D’Andre) Swift’s having a good year and they got (RB Kyle Monangai) 25 back. Certainly know (WR Kalif Raymond) Leaf very well. (WR Rome) Odunze, that whole deal.” Defensive Coordinator: Dennis Allen NFL coaching seasons: 25th season Head coaching seasons : Six (Saints 2022-24, Raiders 2012-14) Defensive coordinator seasons : 10th (Bears 2025-present, Saints 2015-21, Broncos 2011) Previous roles : Senior assistant, secondary coach, Assistant DL coach, Defensive assistant, quality control Influences: Sean Payton, Gregg Williams, John Fox, Jim L. Mora Jr., and Dan Reeves Coached under: Ben Johnson, Payton, Jack Del Rio, Fox, Mora Jr., Reeves Defensive scheme Base : 4-2, attacking 1-gapping front Coverage : Bump-and-run, press-man coverage Staples of scheme : For the season, the Bears use Nickel 60% of the time, with Base 34%, and DIME 6% Since acquiring DT Jeffery Simmons, things have shifted a bit more toward coverage Last three games with Simmons in mix: Nickel 70% of the time, Base 27%, and DIME 3% There has also been a heavier shift from Man to Zone coverage and single-high to two-high sets ZONE: 69% for the season, 77% over the last three games Two-high shell: 52% for the season, 62% over the last three games Results show up in explosive passing plays allowed: 5.2% (2nd best over last three games) On paper, the box score numbers are very good 19.7 points allowed (6th best); 310.5 yards allowed per game (7th); EPA per play: -0.15 (7th) Some of this is because they have the fewest plays against: 542 (fewest in the NFL) However, yards allowed per play: 5.7 (28th); per pass: 7.7 (24th); per run: 4.5 (25th) Hasn’t hurt them overall because they get off the field on 3rd down: 26.6% conversion rate allowed (1st) Historically, have preferred to rush four with DL stunts But have introduced more blitzing in 2026 (35.1%, 10th most) – Double mug (A-gap) Good anticipation of offensive tendencies against blitz Pressures are average: 132 (19th); rate: 37.7% (11th) Sacks are above-average: 32 (4th); rate: 9.1% (2nd) Prioritize stopping the run as a principle Solid overall box score numbers: 94 run yards allowed per game (7th); success rate: 39.6% (6th) Susceptible to explosive runs: 10.5% (17th) and yards before contact: 1.69 (27th) Dan Campbell on the Bears’ defense: “And then defensively, man, they’re playing really good, man. It’s just to continue to grow another year in the system. (DT Jeffery) Simmons is a heck of a player, always has been. That was a good addition for them. (DT) Grady (Jarrett)’s a good player. (EDGE Montez) Sweat. I think (EDGE Austin) Booker has even upped his game in some of the stuff at the overhang and getting (LB Devin) Bush has been big for them, linebacker position. And they have got the corners, (CB) Jaylon (Johnson) and (CB Tyrique) Stevenson over there.”

title: Former Detroit Lions owner Martha Firestone Ford dies at age 101
summary: The Detroit Lions announced on Tuesday night that former team owner Martha Firestone Ford has passed away at age 101. According to the team, she passed away at her home surrounded by family. Ford took over as principal owner of the franchise in 2014, following the death of her husband, William Clay Ford. She held […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 24: Detroit Lions Head Coach Dan Campbell talks with Detroit Lions Owner/Chair Emeritus Martha Firestone Ford during pregame prior to the Detroit Lions versus the Green Bay Packers game on Sunday November 6, 2022 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Detroit Lions announced on Tuesday night that former team owner Martha Firestone Ford has passed away at age 101. According to the team, she passed away at her home surrounded by family. Ford took over as principal owner of the franchise in 2014, following the death of her husband, William Clay Ford. She held onto the role until 2020, when she bequeathed primary ownership to her daughter and current Lions owner Sheila Hamp. Since then, Ford has been serving as Owner/Chair Emeritus of the team. Here’s how the team described her role over the past six years. In her most recent role as Owner/Chair Emeritus, Mrs. Ford supported her four children – Principal Owner/Chair Sheila Ford Hamp, Owner/Vice Chair Martha Ford Morse, Owner/Vice Chair William Clay Ford Jr., and Owner/Vice Chair Elizabeth Ford Kontulis – as they assumed leadership responsibilities within the family franchise. Today the Ford family proudly carries forward the legacy established by Mr. and Mrs. Ford, preserving the values, love, and passion that have shaped a family tradition spanning multiple generations. During Mrs. Ford’s brief stint as primary owner, the Lions made the playoffs twice (2014, 2016) and produced three winning seasons. The team offered this official statement on Ford’s passing: “It is with heavy hearts that we acknowledge the passing of Martha Firestone Ford. Mrs. Ford inspired us all as a pillar of the Detroit community and the passionate matriarch of the Detroit Lions football team. “She will always be remembered for her fierce loyalty to her family, her community, and the city of Detroit. “Her presence on our sideline, in our building, and in our community will be greatly missed. We wish the entire Ford and Firestone families peace in this time of mourning.” For more on Mrs. Ford’s passing and her life accomplishments, check out the Detroit Lions’ official story .

title: Lions, Bears Week 12 injury report: Sam LaPorta, Chuck Clark upgraded on Tuesday
summary: The Detroit Lions (8-2) and Chicago Bears (8-2) will square off in this year’s Thanksgiving Day battle, and for the second straight day, the Lions and Bears have opted for walkthrough practices. full_text: Detroit Lions tight end Sam LaPorta (87) makes a catch against Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (8-2) and Chicago Bears (8-2) will square off in this year’s Thanksgiving Day battle, and for the second straight day, the Lions and Bears have opted for walkthrough practices. A walkthrough practice means that all participation levels are estimates from the coaching staff based on how the player would have participated in a traditional practice. So, with that in mind, let’s look at Tuesday’s injury report and get you up to date on what we know. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded Estimated n o practice DT Skyler Gill-Howard (knee) — Update: His season is over EDGE DJ Wonnum (back) CB Ennis Rakestraw (shoulder) Gill-Howard’s knee injury is significant enough to require surgery and will end his rookie season . A staple of the Lions’ three-man interior defensive line, the Lions will need more production from their depth players beyond starters Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams. “Sky is out for the year. He has a knee injury that will require surgery, so he’ll be out. I hate that for him. He’s had a heck of a season up until this point,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said on Tuesday. Later adding, “He’s done a really good job for us. But we’ve still got Mac (McNeill), we still have Tyleik, we’ve still got Levi (Onwuzurike), we’ve got (Tyler) Lacy that can play in there. Could see (Mekhi) Wingo. We’ve got options there, but you hate to lose a player like him. He’s had a heck of a rookie season.” Wonnum played a full allotment of snaps last Sunday, but his injury appeared to pop up afterward and is significant enough to make him a game-time decision on Thursday, per Campbell. New injuries can be brutal on a short week, but there’s still room for optimism. Rakestraw’s injury kept him out of last weekend’s game, so starting the week with continued restrictions isn’t a great sign for his availability. Campbell didn’t say it directly, but he’ll likely be a game-time decision, too. Estimated limited practice S Chuck Clark (hamstring) — Upgraded from No Practice Clark, like Wonnum, didn’t have a notable injury during Sunday’s game but was estimated to have missed practice on Monday. While it’s an encouraging sign to see him upgraded for Tuesday’s practice, he is also expected to be a game-time decision. Estimated full practice TE Sam LaPorta (ankle) — Upgraded from Limited CB D.J. Reed (hip) CB Khalil Dorsey (wrist) LaPorta was estimated to have been limited on Monday, but would have gotten in a full practice on Tuesday if it had been a traditional practice day. That’s a great sign for his availability on Thursday. Reed continues to improve, but with the Lions taking a slow approach to his recovery, despite the estimated full practices, he’s still likely to be a game-time decision, per Campbell: “Yeah, he’s improving. I mean, I thought he ran around pretty good yesterday. But I can’t give a definitive answer on that just yet. Probably come down, could be game time decision.” Dorsey was injured in the game but returned and played snaps on special teams. With an estimated full practice under his belt, he appears to have a good chance to play on Thursday. summary: The injuries to the Detroit Lions defense are starting to mount. On Tuesday, Lions coach Dan Campbell revealed that rookie defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard is out for the rest of the season with a knee injury sustained during the team’s win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday. Campbell said the injury occurred when Gill-Howard […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-NOVEMBER 22: Defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard (50) of the Detroit Lions looks on from the sidelines during an NFL football game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, November 22, 2026. (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The injuries to the Detroit Lions defense are starting to mount. On Tuesday, Lions coach Dan Campbell revealed that rookie defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard is out for the rest of the season with a knee injury sustained during the team’s win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday. Campbell said the injury occurred when Gill-Howard was in the game during a goal-line play on offense. “Sky is out for the year. He’s out for the year. He had a knee injury that will require surgery. So he’ll be out,” Campbell said. “I hate that for him. He’s had a heck of a season up to this point.” It’s the third significant injury to a Lions defender in the past four weeks, joining linebacker Jack Campbell (neck) and Aidan Hutchinson (torn ACL). Gill-Howard, the team’s sixth-round pick this year, was one of the most pleasant surprises from Detroit’s defense this year. He’s played 316 defensive snaps through 10 games, tallying 2.0 sacks, six quarterback hits, and a tackle for loss. His loss, combined with Hutchinson’s season-ending injury, leaves the Lions a bit shorthanded on the defensive line in terms of pass rushers, but Campbell said it is an opportunity for several players to step up in his absence. “We still got Mac (Alim McNeill), we’ve got Tyleik (Williams), we’ve got Levi (Onwuzurike), we’ve got (Tyler) Lacy who can play in there. It could be (Mekhi) Wingo. Could be Taki (Taimani), could be AK (Aidan Keanaaina). So we’ve got options there,” Campbell said. “But you hate to lose a player like him. He’s had a heck of a rookie season. We’ve mentioned this, but for a young guy, he’s a pro. He’s conscientious in what he did, just the right approach.”

title: NFL Week 12 power rankings: Lions a consensus Top 10 team for first time this season
summary: The Detroit Lions (8-2) are riding a six-game win streak and coming off another strong performance, beating the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 31-21 in a game that wasn’t as close as the score suggests. The Lions land in the Top 10 in every national power ranking for the first time this season, and while most analysts […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell cheers on against Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the second half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (8-2) are riding a six-game win streak and coming off another strong performance, beating the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 31-21 in a game that wasn’t as close as the score suggests. The Lions land in the Top 10 in every national power ranking for the first time this season, and while most analysts are enamored with the offense—specifically superstar Jahmyr Gibbs—many still can’t get past their lack of confidence in the defense. The Lions will have a chance to change that narrative this week when they host the Chicago Bears on Thanksgiving—note: all but one ranker has the Bears ahead of the Lions, save NFL.com—but for now, they’ll remain the underdog . Let’s take a closer look at this week’s national power rankings. NFL.com: 5 (Previous rank: 8) From Nick Shook : Detroit has quietly become one of the most consistent and comfortably predictable teams in the NFL over the last two months, reliably producing offense in a fashion that is thankfully becoming less dependent on Jahmyr Gibbs, while coupling it with a defense that is steadily improving despite new injury losses. The Lions are not as flashy as the 49ers or Bears, nor are they as intimidating as Minnesota’s defense (save for Week 11), but they’re a well-rounded, winning football team that clearly isn’t going away anytime soon. Sunday’s win over the Buccaneers was just another example of this. CBS Sports: 6 (Previous rank: 8) From Pete Prisco : The improvement of the defense is a good sign. They might not have Aidan Hutchinson or Jack Campbell, but they are playing much better on that side of the ball. Sporting News: 6 (Previous rank: 8) From Vinnie Iyer : Jahmyr Gibbs deserves some more MVP discussion. He leads the NFL with 267 touches, 1,098 rushing yards, 1,502 scrimmage yards and 15 total TDs after scoring two more against the Buccaneers. He’s on pace for 2,550 scrimmage yards and 26 TDs, which would be one of the best running back seasons ever. The Athletic: 6 (Previous rank: 9) From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall : Something to be thankful for: Ford Field Only the Bills have won more home games since 2023 than the Lions, who improved to 5-0 at Ford Field on Sunday. They are 26-8 at home since the start of Dan Campbell’s third season. The site of Detroit’s annual Thanksgiving game, where it will be Thursday against the Bears, hasn’t always been so friendly to the home team. From 2000 to 2022, the Lions had the second-lowest home winning percentage in the league (.427). ESPN: 6 (Previous rank: 10) From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard : Extension candidate: S Brian Branch Branch and TE Sam LaPorta are playing out the 2026 season on their four-year rookie deals, but general manager Brad Holmes has reiterated that he would like to reach long-term extensions with both players, though LaPorta has expressed doubts. Branch has made an immediate impact since returning from an Achilles injury that he sustained in Week 7 of last season. In 2026, he has five passes defended and one interception in four games. Depending on how the rest of the season plays out for Branch, the Lions could use the franchise tag or agree to long-term deal with him. USA Today: 7 (Previous rank: 10) From Nate Davis : RB Jahmyr Gibbs will rightly continue to command quite a bit of the spotlight as he keeps trending toward 2,500 yards from scrimmage and potentially breaking Chris Johnson’s single-season record (2,509). But how about a hand for a decimated defense that’s held up pretty well so far without injured stars Aidan Hutchinson and Jack Campbell? Yahoo Sports: 8 (Previous rank: 11) From Frank Schwab : Detroit’s first defensive test without Aidan Hutchinson went well. The Lions allowed just 274 yards and 21 points, and Tampa Bay got 65 yards and a touchdown on a meaningless drive at the end of a game when Detroit led by 17 points. The Lions had four sacks, which was a good sign. The Lions’ defense has been much better since the first few weeks of the season, and Sunday’s game was without Hutchinson and linebacker Jack Campbell. The test Thursday will be tougher, with the Chicago Bears coming in with first place in the NFC North on the line. But if Detroit’s defense can maintain this level, the Lions might be a Super Bowl contender. That could reveal itself on Thanksgiving. “Our guys are competitive, man, and they don’t want to be counted out,” Lions head coach Dan Campbell said of the defense’s performance Sunday, via the team’s site . “And nobody cares. There are no excuses. And the only way to gain respect is just go about your business, man, and make plays and play together and prove your worth, man.” Sports Illustrated: 10 ( Previous rank: 9) From Connor Orr : Dan Campbell has been proven right to this point on Kelvin Sheppard. He stuck by his defensive coordinator, and now his defensive coordinator may see more head coaching interview opportunities based on how well he’s handled all of the adversity foisted onto the Lions’ defense. From Terrion Arnold to Jack Campbell to Aidan Hutchinson…it’s been a long season.

title: Film study: Jahmyr Gibbs in motion creates space for teammates
summary: All Grit. The Detroit Lions won their 6th straight game, knocking off the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, maintaining the top spot in the NFC North. Let’s take a look at those standings. Breathe it in. It feels good. It feels like everything is exactly as it should be. Ben Johnson makes his second return to Ford […]
full_text: Detroit Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing watches a play against Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first half at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 22, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co All Grit. The Detroit Lions won their 6th straight game, knocking off the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, maintaining the top spot in the NFC North. Let’s take a look at those standings. Breathe it in. It feels good. It feels like everything is exactly as it should be. Ben Johnson makes his second return to Ford Field this Thanksgiving, leading the Chicago Bears into town boasting their own 8-2 record. They’re the darlings. The genius head coach. The dynamic quarterback. Every talking head’s favorite team to win the NFC. Good. As our own Ryan Matthews pointed out, Jared Goff looks and acts just as good as the real thing—the MVP quarterbacks who garner all of the attention—but his name isn’t Joe or Josh. That same misfit-toys metaphor applies to Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing compared to Johnson. Sure, he might be a little shorter in stature and has been given the nickname “Megamind,” but Petzing’s offense looks and plays just as well as Ben the boy wonder’s. And if Petzing keeps getting overlooked nationally, the Lions could be fortunate enough to keep their offensive coordinator for the foreseeable future. If the stigma of his three-year stint as the playcaller in Arizona stays with him, good. Detroit will gladly retain him. For this film study, I want to put one play design element under the microscope: presnap motion. Not just any presnap motion, but utilizing the NFL’s best offensive weapon to create space. Stretching the seams Todd Bowles and the Buccaneers’ defensive unit have a history of being stout, resulting in frustrating matchups for some of the NFL’s most prolific offenses. Just peek at Caleb Williams’s Week 9 box score against the Bucs: 22-for-37 with 2 touchdowns, 4 interceptions, and a cool 61.5 passer rating. Petzing and Goff, however, diagnosed Bowles’ tendencies and stressed them. The key to it all: Jahmyr Gibbs. I don’t need to tell anyone reading this how spectacular Gibbs is with the football. But the best part of his game this weekend was how he impacted the defense without the ball. The first two plays below are the exact same concept. Starting in shotgun with Gibbs to Goff’s right, the running back is sent in motion to the short side of the field toward an in-line tight end (Brock Wright) and Amon-Ra St. Brown outside the numbers. The cool part of the design is in the details. Watch how Gibbs ’ wheel/fade route is run. Notably, Gibbs angles his route very wide toward the sideline hash marks, rather than pressing vertical quickly. The key here is that it forces the cover-3 cornerback to keep his drop wide, opening space for the tight end seam route. The other key here is utilizing Jameson Williams on the field-side slot and Isaac TeSlaa outside the numbers. The passing strength of the offense, pre-motion, is to the top field-side of the screen with three eligible receivers. TeSlaa, Williams, and Gibbs. With the motion, the passing strength changes, moving the trips side to the short side. The middle single-high safety now has a choice: stay on the field-side hash to protect against Jameson Williams in the slot vertical, or lean to the now trips side with the Gibbs motion. Good luck. Either way, he’s wrong. On the second time below, Petzing calls the same play, but the defense tries to correct. Notice how the cover-3 short-side corner cheats inside for the tight end vertical, but at the last second tries to shift back toward Gibbs. Goff recognizes this correction and checks down to the safety valve of St. Brown, who sides in the flat for a positive play. Same idea, different look Looking back at the opening series of the game, Petzing clearly had this intent of putting Gibbs in motion to stress the vertical seams in the Bucs’ zone coverage. This time, Petzing causes the same stress using the same concept of motioning Gibbs out of the backfield, but this time from a shotgun two-back look (although the second back is actually a tight end, who runs the delayed hook route into the cleared-out zone). But again, notice how wide Gibbs’ route is run, ultimately fading to the outside hashes. The details create the space just as much as the threat of his athleticism. Further, notice that on all three of these plays, Gibbs’ route and the tight end’s route are all run with similar depth and pacing despite having different speeds. The coverage is stressed with precision timing. Details are the difference between good offensive coordinators and great ones. There are many coaches that can draw up a great scheme on the chalkboard Monday-Saturday. But translating speed and space from the chalkboard to the field requires precision details with a championship-level mindset. Influencing the linebackers Lastly, a different pre-snap motion, but with the same focus of influencing defenders to open up space. This time, the goal is to influence the linebackers and create space in the zone for Amon-Ra St. Brown. Notice how quickly Alex Anzalone reacts to the motion to get horizontal from the field-side linebacker position. St. Brown is able to swiftly find and sit in the opening created for an easy pitch-and-catch. It’s a short week with the Bears coming in on Thursday for the big Thanksgiving showdown. But even with less practice time to prepare, I expect Petzing will have his wrinkle of the week, targeting what Dan, Drew, Jared, and the rest of the offensive staff diagnose as the weakness and tendency of the Bears’ defense. Embrace the fight. Appreciate the opportunity. Keep the edge.

title: Packers Week 12 Opponent Preview: Who are this year’s Los Angeles Rams?
summary: The Green Bay Packers and Los Angeles Rams head into Wednesday’s Week 12 matchup with matching 6-4 records, but they arrive headed in opposite directions. The Rams have won four straight, and their defense has allowed three touchdowns in five games, the fewest in the NFL. Green Bay lost 30-10 at home to Minnesota in […]
full_text: Nov 5, 2023; Green Bay, Wisconsin, USA; Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay greets Green Bay Packers head coach Matt LaFleur following the game at Lambeau Field. Mandatory Credit: Jeff Hanisch-USA TODAY Sports | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Green Bay Packers and Los Angeles Rams head into Wednesday’s Week 12 matchup with matching 6-4 records, but they arrive headed in opposite directions. The Rams have won four straight, and their defense has allowed three touchdowns in five games, the fewest in the NFL. Green Bay lost 30-10 at home to Minnesota in their last game. Both teams are still trying to find some identity and could best be described as playoff bubble teams at this stage of the season. The Packers have a chance to close the gap on Minnesota in the division with the Vikings’ loss to San Francisco last Sunday night, whereas the Rams likely won’t even catch their division rivals in that regard as the 49ers continue to widen the gap on them. The Rams rebuilt their pass rush around Myles Garrett and a returning Aaron Donald and rank 2nd in defensive EPA/play. On offense they are missing Puka Nacua (out for the season) and Davante Adams (IR). Micah Parsons is cleared to make his 2026 debut for Green Bay. 2025 recap Los Angeles went 12-5 and reached the NFC Championship Game, where they lost in a shootout to Seattle. The offense was the league’s best by EPA/play (0.11, 1st), with 0.21 EPA per dropback and a 50.7% success rate. The defense ranked 11th in EPA/play allowed (-0.08). Then the Rams spent the offseason going all in on defense. Key losses Edge Jared Verse was traded to Cleveland in the Myles Garrett deal. OC Mike LaFleur left to become Arizona’s head coach. Assistant head coach Aubrey Pleasant was not retained. Senior offensive assistant Alex Van Pelt left for Atlanta. CB Cobie Durant and CB Derion Kendrick signed with Dallas. OT Rob Havenstein and CB Darious Williams retired. QB Jimmy Garoppolo left. CB Roger McCreary, LB Troy Reeder, CB Ahkello Witherspoon, T D.J. Humphries and TE Nick Vannett also left. TE Mark Redman was traded to Green Bay for a 2028 seventh-round pick. Key additions Edge Myles Garrett was acquired from Cleveland for Verse, a 2027 first, a 2028 second and a conditional 2029 third. CB Trent McDuffie was acquired from Kansas City for picks and signed a 4-year, $124M extension. DT Aaron Donald came out of retirement on a 1-year, $20M deal. CB Jaylen Watson signed for 3 years, $51M. LB Grant Stuard signed for 2 years, $4.45M. WR Tutu Atwell was reacquired from Miami. QB Matthew Stafford re-signed for 1 year, $55M. S Kamren Curl re-signed for 3 years, $36M. TE Tyler Higbee re-signed for 2 years, $6M. OC Nathan Scheelhaase was promoted from pass game coordinator. Assistant head coach Kliff Kingsbury joined the staff. Special teams coordinator Bubba Ventrone joined the staff. QB Ty Simpson was a 1st-round pick (No. 13). TE Max Klare was a 2nd-round pick. OT Keagen Trost was a 3rd-round pick. Chris Shula remains defensive coordinator, and Sean McVay still calls plays. Efficiency, 2026 through Week 11 Rams offense EPA/play: 0.04 (8th) EPA/dropback: 0.08 (~10th) EPA/rush: 0.00 (~6th) Success rate: 49.0% (3rd) Points per game: 24.8 Rams defense EPA/play allowed: -0.16 (2nd) EPA/dropback allowed: -0.19 (2nd) EPA/rush allowed: -0.11 (~6th) Success rate allowed: 40.9% (~9th) Points allowed per game: 18.7 Touchdowns allowed, last five games: 3 (fewest in NFL) Packers offense EPA/play: -0.03 (14th) EPA/dropback: 0.09 (9th) EPA/rush: -0.26 (32nd) Success rate: 39.7% (~27th) Completions of 20-plus yards: 43 (1st) Packers defense EPA/play allowed: -0.11 (8th) EPA/dropback allowed: -0.12 (~8th) EPA/rush allowed: -0.09 (~12th) Success rate allowed: 43.3% Rams 2025 (full season) Offense EPA/play: 0.11 (1st) Offense EPA/dropback: 0.21 Offense EPA/rush: -0.02 Offense success rate: 50.7% (1st) Defense EPA/play allowed: -0.08 (11th) Defense EPA/dropback allowed: -0.10 Defense EPA/rush allowed: -0.06 Defense success rate allowed: 41.5% First ten games L 7-27 at SF (Melbourne) W 28-6 vs. NYG L 26-30 at DEN W 24-20 at PHI L 34-37 (OT) vs. BUF L 16-18 vs. ARI W 35-21 at LV W 24-9 vs. LAC W 20-13 at WAS W 34-6 at ARI: the line had its best game despite losing guard Steve Avila, center Coleman Shelton and backup Dylan McMahon. McVay used 20 personnel 17 times with a 59% success rate. Week 11: bye Keys for Green Bay Protect Love against the best front he’ll see this season. Garrett, Donald, Kobie Turner (back from a groin injury), Byron Young and Braden Fiske give the Rams five real pass rushers. Love throws about 36 times a game, and the Packers can’t run the ball, so they have to win with quick throws and help for the tackles. Keep taking deep shots. Love leads the NFL in 20-plus-yard completions, and Christian Watson (916 yards) and Matthew Golden (853 yards) have combined for over 1,700 yards. A secondary built around McDuffie and Watson will make those throws hard, but the big plays are Green Bay’s offense. Make Stafford beat you without his best receiver. With Nacua and Adams out, Higbee is the Rams’ leading receiver with only 304 yards. Stafford has thrown 10 interceptions. Parsons has 3 sacks in two career games against Stafford, and Jonathan Gannon should test a patched-up offensive line. Don’t get out-schemed in the run game. The Rams rank about 6th in EPA per rush and succeed on 49% of plays, 3rd in the league. McVay is now leaning on two-back looks, so stopping the run on early downs keeps Stafford in obvious passing downs. Win the margins. At 44, this is the lowest total of any Packers preview this season. Against a defense this good, field position, takeaways and red-zone touchdowns instead of field goals will decide it. Injuries to watch: For Los Angeles, Puka Nacua and TE Terrance Ferguson are out for the season, Davante Adams is on IR, and guards Steve Avila and Coleman Shelton are out. For Green Bay, Micah Parsons is expected to make his season debut.

title: Rams break out new 20 personnel package ahead of Packers game
summary: Sean McVay has made a habit of turning injuries into new ideas. Last season, when injuries hit the Los Angeles Rams’ wide receivers, he leaned heavily on 13 personnel, using three tight ends to keep the offense moving. This year, injuries have hit both receiver and tight end, and McVay’s answer is a 20 personnel […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - OCTOBER 6: Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) back to pass during the NFL game between the Green Bay Packers and the Los Angeles Rams on October 06, 2024, at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, CA. (Photo by Jevone Moore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Sean McVay has made a habit of turning injuries into new ideas. Last season, when injuries hit the Los Angeles Rams’ wide receivers, he leaned heavily on 13 personnel, using three tight ends to keep the offense moving. This year, injuries have hit both receiver and tight end, and McVay’s answer is a 20 personnel package with two running backs, no tight ends and three receivers. Players said it wasn’t installed until the Monday before the Rams’ week 10 game, but they still had 17 plays in the “Pony” package ready by the following Sunday, and they covered a lot of ground. “Pony” personnel is two running backs instead of the traditional running back/fullback combination. 20 personnel is two backs, zero tight ends, three wide receivers. In the diagram above, there are no tight ends. The package is a good example of the “illusion of complexity.” Most of the calls were designed passes, and with only three vertical threats at the snap, it shouldn’t have stressed a defense much on paper. In practice, it did. Between the motion, the split-back alignment and a variety of protections, defenders had to account for the entire field on almost every snap. The package started with a run-pass option. Kyren Williams motioned out of the backfield on a bubble route, and the defense didn’t adjust in time. That gave the quarterback an easy choice. On one side, two receivers were blocking two defensive backs for Williams in space. On the other, he would have been handing off into a seven-man box with only five blockers. The ball went outside, as it should have. If the Rams develop a run game in this package, this is a natural place to start. The run side is mid zone, a scheme the line has blocked for years, and the bubble gives the defense a reason to stay honest. The second play was a staple Rams passing concept, a variant of their corner-choice concept. Since Williams is one of the best running backs in the NFL at running choice routes, here he is given a two-way go and reads the defender over him and breaks inside or outside based on leverage. He can also sit the route down between the zone defenders. Normally, sending the back out on that route means giving up a blocker. From split backs, though, the second back stays in, so the Rams keep six-man protection while Williams runs the route. It ended up as a drop but expect to see this one again. Later on, the Rams came back to the same concept but flipped. This time, the Cardinals were playing split safety cover-6 with cover-2 to the backside to take away the choice route underneath. Stafford saw this and threw the vertical route hole shot into the cover-2 void between the corner and safety. Another passing variant they can run from this formation is the stick/flat/mini dagger concept. This play design is a design the Packers love to run as well. Stafford hit a no-look throw here to the crossing route on the mini dagger side. The split-back alignment also gives the Rams more flexibility in protection. They can slide six-man protection to either side, depending on where the biggest threat lines up. They can also use their usual double-chip protection in a new way. Usually, a tight end chips one edge rusher and the back chips the other. With two backs in the backfield, each one can chip the rusher on his side before releasing, which gives deeper routes more time to develop. When the Rams want more players running routes, they can go to five-man protection and use one of the backs as the flat-control route. Most passing concepts need someone working underneath to the flat, and the backfield is a natural place to run it from. The defense sees two backs, and either one could be blocking, chipping or running a route. As usual with McVay, there were several screens built off motion. The best was a middle screen behind a flare motion by the running back. When the back released toward the sideline, the cornerback started backing up, and the motion pulled his eyes away from the receiver in front of him. By the time the receiver caught the ball, an offensive lineman was already coming at the defender, and the screen worked exactly as designed. What makes the package impressive isn’t just the plays. It’s how quickly it came together. McVay didn’t rebuild his offense to use 20 personnel. He took concepts the Rams already run with other personnel groupings and adapted them to two backs. The bubble RPO uses the same mid zone the line already knows. The protections follow the same rules with different players. The screens use the same motions the Rams have used for years. It looks new, but it’s built from familiar pieces, and that’s why a package installed on Monday could work on Sunday. The bigger question is where it goes from here and what will the Packers see. A two-back package with Williams as the main weapon has been a long time coming. If McVay adds a real run game to what he showed this past week, the injuries that forced this change could end up giving the Rams a lasting new wrinkle in their offense.

title: Green Bay Packers News: What does the defense look like with Micah Parsons?
summary: Micah Parsons is back. What does that actually mean? Presumably having the perennial All-Pro back in the lineup will be a boost for the pass rush, but the way in which Parsons is actually used is still unknown. Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has been creative in his personnel usage so far this year; the Packers’ […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - DECEMBER 07: Micah Parsons #1 of the Green Bay Packers looks on against the Chicago Bears during the second quarter at Lambeau Field on December 07, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Micah Parsons is back. What does that actually mean? Presumably having the perennial All-Pro back in the lineup will be a boost for the pass rush, but the way in which Parsons is actually used is still unknown. Defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon has been creative in his personnel usage so far this year; the Packers’ safety room is the perfect example. Gannon has seemingly unlocked the best versions of Xavier McKinney, Evan Williams, and Javon Bullard, and all three were already good and useful players before Gannon came along. What would the same sort of application look like for Parsons? We can’t know the answer to that yet, but from a tactical perspective I’d bet the defense looks broadly similar with Parsons on the field. I don’t think Gannon, who has achieved success with an aggressive and frequently exotic blitz package, is going to dial everything back just because Parsons is there to provide, hopefully, a boost to the non-blitz pass rush. Once Parsons gets his feet under him, the defense will hopefully be a marriage of Parsons’ maniacal and relentless pass rush with Gannon’s schematic trickery. Hopefully, the ultimate answer to “what does the Packers’ defense look like with Micah Parsons on the field” is “significantly better,” whatever form that actually takes. And make no mistake, the defense without Parsons has still been plenty good. He may not be able to fix the offensive line, but if Parsons can take the defense to another level, maybe that’s enough to help this Packers team achieve its full potential. title: Despite everything, the Packers still have their goals within reach
summary: I’d like to say 2026 has been a uniquely stupid year of Packers football, but I don’t know if that’s true. Certainly there have been uniquely stupid aspects of it; I can’t think of another year where the Packers have taken such drastic steps to find someone, anyone capable of playing replacement-level football on their […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 15: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers passes the ball against the Minnesota Vikings during the second quarter at Lambeau Field on November 15, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’d like to say 2026 has been a uniquely stupid year of Packers football, but I don’t know if that’s true. Certainly there have been uniquely stupid aspects of it; I can’t think of another year where the Packers have taken such drastic steps to find someone, anyone capable of playing replacement-level football on their offensive line during the season. I can’t think of another season where the Packers have had a comparable cavalcade of injuries, except for maybe 2025. Maybe that’s just modern football. I don’t know. I can’t think of another season where so many games have been, if not just affected, seemingly outright steered toward an outcome by the officials. But handwaving all of that, let’s just say it’s been a stupid year. If not uniquely so, I think we can land on that. And yet! Here the Packers sit entering Week 12 with everything they want still within reach. If the season ended today, the Packers would make the playoffs, occupying the seventh seed in the NFC field, a position that will surely one day be named for Matt LaFleur. The Rams and Seahawks are hot on their tails, but a win this week — certainly very achievable against an injury-diminished Rams squad — would solidify their lead over both teams. They’d widen their lead over the Seahawks by strengthening their conference record and put a serious dent in the Rams’ chances by taking ownership of the head-to-head tiebreaker. And if the Packers make the playoffs, who knows what could happen? Right now, the playoff field would see them matched up against the Detroit Lions in the wildcard round. That, too, is an eminently winnable game. The Packers had the Lions all but dead to rights in Week 7 but for their semi-permanent kicking woes. And even so, if Josh Jacobs takes the small but significant step of simply catching the ball in the end zone, there’s a very good chance they beat the Lions. I think outside of the Vikings, the Packers could at least be competitive against pretty much any team in the NFC. There are certainly some talented teams in the field, but none of them have the borderline psychopathy of Brian Flores. If that’s what it takes to beat the Packers (other than a kicker meltdown), you have to at least think the Packers have a chance. And I suppose that’s the point I’m trying to make here. The Packers still have virtually everything to play for and all of it is within their control. The NFC North title might be out of reach, but the playoffs are still fully achievable. The Packers control their own destiny on every front; keep winning and they’re in the playoffs. Stumble and their odds grow more remote by the week. But it’s all up to the Packers. They’ve shown this year that they can beat anyone — or lose to just about anyone, too. Their weaknesses are almost entirely self inflicted, but the solutions to those weaknesses are all self-driven, too. There are a lot of different ways you could spin this Packers season, but I think the ultimate story is that this is a team that had everything within its grasp, despite whatever weirdness befell them. And that fact may end up being the biggest indictment anyone can level against the 2026 Green Bay Packers.

title: Packers activate Micah Parsons from PUP list to 53-man roster
summary: 11 months and 10 days. That’s the amount of time it took for Micah Parsons to return to the Green Bay Packers’ active roster after suffering a torn ACL (and other damage to his knee) late in the 2025 season. As of Tuesday, Parsons is back on the 53, with the Packers officially processing his […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - SEPTEMBER 24: Micah Parsons #1 of the Green Bay Packers walks the field during warm-up prior to the game against the Atlanta Falcons at Lambeau Field on September 24, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images 11 months and 10 days. That’s the amount of time it took for Micah Parsons to return to the Green Bay Packers’ active roster after suffering a torn ACL (and other damage to his knee) late in the 2025 season. As of Tuesday, Parsons is back on the 53, with the Packers officially processing his return to active duty this afternoon. Green Bay had an open spot on the roster ready for Parsons, having released running back Pierre Strong, Jr. a few days ago, so no corresponding move was necessary. Despite missing three games in 2025, Parsons was named a first-team All-Pro in his initial season with the Green and Gold. His 12.5 sacks led the Packers last season and was the highest total for a Packers defender over a full season since Za’Darius Smith put up 13.5 in 2019. Eight of Parsons’ sacks came in the fourth quarter or overtime as well, demonstrating his value to the team in crunch time. Without Parsons, the Packers’ defense took a significant step back at the end of 2025, giving up at least 360 yards in each of the four games he missed. However, the unit — and the pass rush in particular — has taken a giant leap forward in 2026 under new coordinator Jonathan Gannon. The Packers rank first in the NFL in turnover rate and they are third in the league in net yards per pass attempt allowed. Furthermore, their sack numbers have skyrocketed despite Parsons’ absence; 2025 saw the team record just 36 sacks over 17 games, including Parsons’ 12.5, but this year, the team is already up to 29 through just 10 games. And now, the biggest veteran addition that the Packers have made in decades is back and ready to wreak havoc in backfields once again. Parsons is officially listed as questionable for Wednesday’s game against the Los Angeles Rams, but that should be a formality. His ramp-up period is now behind him, and by all accounts, he’s ready to go give a boost to a squad that’s looking to go on a strong stretch run.

title: Week 12 Power Rankings Round Up: Packers idle week keeps team steady
summary: The Green Bay Packers’ bye week has come and gone, and Green Bay will kick off Week 12 on Wednesday night in the NFL’s first Thanksgiving Eve game. The team was already back in town over the weekend, preparing for the Rams, also coming off their bye week. Green Bay is 4-3 in the game […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ bye week has come and gone, and Green Bay will kick off Week 12 on Wednesday night in the NFL’s first Thanksgiving Eve game. The team was already back in town over the weekend, preparing for the Rams, also coming off their bye week. Green Bay is 4-3 in the game after the bye week under Matt LaFleur, with this week’s contest being as much of a “must-win” as any November game can be. Collectively, we are still trying to figure out who this squad is, as we have seen a rollercoaster ride of the highs and lows with this team. Los Angeles isn’t necessarily the same team they were the last couple seasons, but still present as a formidable opponent. The Rams have already ruled out two of their starting offensive linemen, tight end Terrance Ferguson, and Puka Nacua. As fortunate as that is for Green Bay, Myles Garrett and Aaron Donaldson will still be on the defensive line against whatever the Packers can trot out on the front five. In the eyes of those around the league, Green Bay didn’t really move in the various Power Rankings pieces. The team was on bye, so they didn’t lose any ground this week, but the team didn’t win either, so they didn’t gain any ground either. Around the division, Chicago and Detroit both won this week, and the Vikings fell in Mexico City. With Micah Parsons set to return this week, let’s see what the writers around the league think of the Packers. NFL Power Rankings Entering Week 12 : NFL.com: 11th For a second consecutive week, NFL.com’s Nick Shook is the highest on the Packers, though he did drop the team one spot to 11th. The Giants’ win over the Jaguars was enough to propel the NFC East leaders from 16 to 10. On the Packers, though, Shook writes: “The bye came at a good time for the Packers, who entered the week off licking their wounds after being outclassed by the Vikings at Lambeau Field. Facing a two-game deficit in the NFC North, they’ll have to prove they’ve recovered quickly on Wednesday night against the Rams in order to stay within striking distance in the division race.” Fox Sports: 12th ESPN: 12th CBS Sports: 12th Bleacher Report: 12th Sports Illustrated: 12th USA Today: 12th Yahoo Sports: 13th Pro Football Talk: 13th The Athletic: 13th Green Bay is ranked consistently in the 12th or 13th spot in this week’s rankings. In The Athletic ’s rankings, with a Thanksgiving theme, Josh Kendall and Chad Graff write: “Something to be thankful for: Good health Specifically that of Micah Parsons, who could make his season debut this week after missing 13 games due to a torn ACL suffered in Week 15 last year. Putting the three-time All-Pro back onto a defense that is already top 10 in sacks (29), EPA (4.2 per 100 snaps) and yards per play allowed (4.9) gives the Packers a shot to survive the league’s toughest division. Green Bay is in last place in the NFC North but still has a 35 percent chance of making the playoffs.” So all in all, there is hope for the Packers yet. A win would go a long way this week and give the Green Bay players an additional “mini bye” ahead of next week’s contest against the Saints.

title: Packers list 8 players as questionable for Rams game
summary: Officially, Micah Parsons is listed as questionable for Wednesday’s game between the Green Bay Packers and the Los Angeles Rams. Unofficially, it would be a total shock if Parsons would not be activated from the PUP list and would not suit up in the game. Parsons has been building towards a return in this game […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - AUGUST 13: Sean Rhyan #75 of the Green Bay Packers in action against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Officially, Micah Parsons is listed as questionable for Wednesday’s game between the Green Bay Packers and the Los Angeles Rams. Unofficially, it would be a total shock if Parsons would not be activated from the PUP list and would not suit up in the game. Parsons has been building towards a return in this game for three weeks, and with his return to practice window officially closing on Wednesday, it’s time to put him back on the 53-man roster. All indications are that Parsons is ready to go, and his presence will surely be a boost to a defense that has found a solid pass rush even without him this season. But beyond Parsons’ status of questionable, the Packers have another seven players with that designation — and, notably, none with a status of doubtful or out for the game. Among that group are multiple likely starters, including a pair on the offensive line in Sean Rhyan and Kevin Zeitler. Rhyan appears set to make his return on Wednesday after missing three games with an ankle injury. Zeitler, meanwhile, was gearing up to make his first start as a Packer in Week 10, but a triceps injury suffered in practice cost him that chance. Look for those two to be in the lineup at center and right guard barring any further unexpected issues with their recovery. Meanwhile, the Packers also have starting linebacker Zaire Franklin on the comeback trail after he missed the last four games. Franklin’s hairline fracture in his leg was another bizarre practice injury, and his return would be a welcome sight against a Rams running game that ranks among the league’s better units. Other questionable players include running back Josh Jacobs, wide receivers Bo Melton and Skyy Moore, and offensive lineman Travis Glover. Jacobs appears to be the one true question mark based on Matt LaFleur’s comments this week, as his broken finger could affect his ability to secure the football. The team has also missed Moore on special teams, with the return game suffering significantly since he was injured back in week five. Moore was also knocked out of the Packers’ last game against Minnesota, but appears ready to get back at it as a return man and slot receiver option. Notable omissions from the injury report include guard Aaron Banks, cornerback Brandon Cisse, and linebacker Isaiah McDuffie. All were assigned practice statuses leading up to this game, with Cisse having dropped out of the Vikings game in Week 10, but all finished the week as full participants in practice and should be set to play on Wednesday. All eyes will again be on the interior of the offensive line in warmups on Wednesday, as the team could end up going with Banks, Rhyan, and Zeitler in a fully new-look group. However, if Banks still cannot crack the starting lineup despite evidently being fully healthy (by midseason standards), that should illustrate just what the coaching staff thinks of him at this point. Stay tuned for the list of gameday inactives that should come out 90 minutes before kickoff and for news on Parsons’ expected return to the 53-man roster sometime on Tuesday or Wednesday afternoon.

title: Texans fans can give thanks for…
summary: In the spirit of Thanksgiving, let’s put together a list of things Houston Texans fans can and should be thankful for as the team dances around the In/Out line of the 2026 NFL Playoffs. As frustrating as this season has been so far, it could certainly be worse – the McNair’s could have moved to […]
full_text: In the spirit of Thanksgiving, let’s put together a list of things Houston Texans fans can and should be thankful for as the team dances around the In/Out line of the 2026 NFL Playoffs. As frustrating as this season has been so far, it could certainly be worse – the McNair’s could have moved to Nashville and sold the team to [NAME REDACTED]. Quarterback C.J. Stroud Stroud caught a ton of flack last season, particularly at the end when the New England Patriots walked off with a victory and the Texans went home. Stroud responded by showing up early in the off-season, staying late, putting in the work to be the best Texan he could be and >boom< the dude is elite now. Making a cut-up of all of C.J. Stroud’s 22 TD passes and realized nearly all of them had little to no YAC so I did some digging on the numbers. Pretty impressive stuff. Cut-up 🔜 pic.twitter.com/kSwnThr5kf — Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) November 24, 2026 C.J. Stroud leads the pack 👀 pic.twitter.com/8hQH8On8HR — PFF (@PFF) November 20, 2026 10 games into the season, Stroud has thrown 347 passes for 222 completions for a 64.0 completion percentage and 2656 yards. He’s also nailed 124 first downs, 22 touchdowns, given away only 4 picks and has his highest career passer rating to date at 103.6 with a 73 QBR. And he’s done all this with bad schemes, poor play calling, a non-existent run game, average-to-terrible pass blocking and a rotating cast of available teammates. NFL insider Jason LaCanfora recently dropped an article predicting a big payday for Stroud, after he turned down Nick Caserio’s contract extension offer before the season started. Jason LaCanfora on Casino.org The Texans had a slew of injuries on defense, but it’s hard for people around the league to get their heads around how dramatically that unit has fallen apart. All the while, QB C.J. Stroud is making the case for a $60 million-a-year contract. “I thought he made a mistake at the time,” one personnel exec said of Stroud rejecting Houston’s overtures before the season, “but he is going to take them to the bank.” Another personnel exec opined: “If you put this version of Stroud with that defense last year, Houston wins the Super Bowl.” Hard to argue with that. At last Thursday’s game, a sideline reported noted they spoke to Caserio who said the plan is to lock down Stroud for the rest of his career as soon as this year’s campaign comes to an end. #Stroud4life So when you’re sitting around giving thanks tomorrow – raise a glass to C.J. Stroud. Will Anderson Jr. is trying to outdo Stroud Say what you will about Caserio’s (and Cole Popovich and Nick Caley’s) inability to build and execute an elite offensive line, but ole Nick nailed it when he pulled off the draft steal of the century and landed Stroud and Anderson Jr. back to back. So far in 2026, WAJ has been a 1-man wrecking crew, terrorizing offensive linemen in ways that has J.J Watt cheering, opposing players and coaches cringing and pundits clamoring for him to get the Defensive Player of the Year award when this season ends. Will his safety in last Thursdays game against the Indianapolis Colts, WAJ now has 11.5 sacks in 2026, cleanly in the #1 spot for that stat. In his short career, he’s almost at 50 – a number he might hit before this (only his 4th season) ends. Will Anderson Jr sacks by season Games 2023 7.0 13 2024 11.0 14 2025 12.0 17 2026 11.5 10 pic.twitter.com/Siy6vCbxPC — PFF (@PFF) November 20, 2026 He’s also dominating almost every other meaningful category for a defender: Will Anderson Jr.’s 2026 season through 11 weeks via @PFF : 55 Pressures (2nd) 14 Sacks (1st) 92.0 PFF Grade (1st) 90.7 RDEF Grade (1st) 90.2 PRSH Grade (2nd) 30 Defensive Stops (1st) 3 Fumbles Forced (T-2nd) The heavy favorite to win his first DPOY this year. — Jacob Barzilla (@JacobBarzilla) November 24, 2026 Will Anderson Jr. was in the Colts backfield all night. 5 TKL, 2 TFL, 1 SACK, 4 QBH, 1 SAFETY. Anderson is looking more and more like the player to beat for Defensive Player of the Year. https://t.co/FxNHpVS9Gp pic.twitter.com/PYLeYo5C15 — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 20, 2026 Let’s all give thanks for Will Anderson Jr.! The Houston Texans are favored to land a wild card spot With all the off-season and pre-season hype around this team, no one expected them to have a 4-6 record right now. The decision to alter the defensive scheme for 2026 has clearly backfired on DC Matt Burke and head coach Demeco Ryans. The lack of a run game shouldn’t surprise anyone who’s been paying attention to Nick Caley’s offense, but when David Montgomery gets going, he’s proven he (and a healthy Woody Marks) can make chicken salad from chicken [BLEEP]. Especially when defenses are concerned about Stroud carving them up like a John Madden Turducken. However, as it sits right now, the Texans are the favorites for the 7th and final spot in the AFC race. And, with one of the easiest remaining schedules , a roster dripping with talent, and (hopefully) a few lucky breaks, they can still actually win the division. The Jacksonville Jaguars are currently in 1st place at 7-3, but Glitter Kitties gonna Glitter, and they could easily drop enough remaining games to find themselves in wild card land, if not out altogether. Unfortunately for us, the Jaguars have an even easier remaining schedule than H-Town. However, the Texans are 3-1 against the division right now, while the Jags are 2-1. If Houston wins out they land at 11-6, if Jacksonville loses to the Pittsburgh Steelers and the division opponents, Houston owns the tie breaker. A lot of lucky ball bounces have to happen in that scenario, but this is pro ball and crazy things happen every weekend. What Texans thing are you most thankful for?
